articles.title: US judge strikes down Trump immigrant visa ban affecting 75 countries
articles.summary: A federal judge in Manhattan ruled against the State Department’s suspension of immigrant visas.
articles.body:
A United States judge has struck down a policy introduced by the administration of President Donald Trump suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, saying the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority.

Judge Jeannette Vargas of Manhattan said in her ruling on Friday in the Southern District of New York that the policy was “patently unlawful” and conflicted with federal immigration law, which explicitly stripped the secretary of state of authority over consular officers’ adjudication of immigrant visas.

“The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote.

Vargas, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden, issued the ruling in a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together, along with applicants for immigrant visas and US citizens sponsoring family members from the designated countries.

The suspension, which took effect in January of this year, affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil , Colombia and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh; and many nations in Africa , the Middle East and the Caribbean.

The Department of State said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”.

President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown during his presidency that he argues is aimed at improving domestic security. According to the Center for Constitutional Rights, the freeze was one of several restrictions the administration has imposed in rapid succession, following a broader travel ban covering 39 countries that took effect January 1, and a pause on diversity visa issuance in late December.

Rights groups have suggested that the crackdown violates free speech and due process rights, particularly for minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The State Department has not yet commented on the ruling.

articles.title: Quiet on set. How AI transformed China’s microdrama scene
articles.summary: The breakneck AI transformation of the industry is the kind of technological disruption that many creatives fear could upend movie-making far beyond China.
articles.body: Everything seemed to be business as usual as filming got underway on a dimly lit set in a basement in Hengdian, a town nicknamed “China’s Hollywood” for its sprawling complex of film studios. Cameramen raced around hectically setting up lights and checking shots as choreographers ran through fight sequences and a prop team worked out how to hoist a net that would later restrain a hostage. Actors, most dressed as assassins and hitmen, milled about or squatted, smoking cigarettes and getting occasional touch-ups from roving hair stylists and make-up artists as they waited for their scene to start. But behind the bustle was a new reality: while just a few months ago, production of these so-called “microdramas” was flourishing in Hengdian and other hubs – today, these sets are falling quiet. Seemingly overnight, new AI-video generation tools have taken over the microdrama industry, able to produce these popular, vertical shows at a fraction of the cost, decimating the number of live-action productions across the country and flooding platforms with AI-made content. More than 120,000 microdramas were released in the first three months of this year — with 95% of those generated by AI, according to Chinese state media. That’s made the industry one of the most visible examples of how China’s breakneck AI transformation is impacting people’s livelihoods — wiping out jobs and creating new ones, leaving everyone unsure what’s next. It’s the kind of technological disruption that many creatives fear could upend movie-making far beyond China. Between takes actor Junlin, who asked to be identified by her stage name, talks about how she’s struggling to stay afloat as a “bitter winter” has arrived for productions like hers. “With fewer productions hiring, your space for survival is constantly squeezed,” said the 24-year-old, dressed in combat boots and a high ponytail to play a head assassin who storms around with a posse of hitmen in an upcoming microdrama. She’d worked only seven days in June, a sharp fall from the spring when she’d been filming 25 out of about 30 days per month in Hengdian and other cities. “I’m someone who gets anxious easily,” she said. “If I’m not on set, I would be in a constant state of anxiety.” Boom time Hengdian, a town of just over 200,000 tucked in a rural part of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, had been booming with the rise of the microdrama industry in recent years. Broken into roughly 90-second episodes, microdramas first emerged during the pandemic, capitalizing on the popularity of short video apps like Douyin and Kuaishou as cinemas and studios closed. While each episode is designed to be quick to consume on a mobile phone, together the clips weave together plotlines that can stretch the length of a feature film. These microdramas — and their often soapy or outlandish plots about wicked mother-in-laws, mistaken identities, wartime heroics and wronged lovers — have since proliferated in China and spread to audiences overseas, where they’ve spawned a fast-growing, multi-billion-dollar industry. They’ve also caught the attention of China’s censors, who are tightening oversight of microdramas with new rules set to take effect in September. Plotlines, for example, will need to “adhere to correct political direction.” Last year, the domestic microdrama industry was valued at nearly $15 billion, according to market research firm DataEye, almost double the market size for box-office feature films in the country. Its rise ushered in a welcome heyday for young creatives at a time of high youth unemployment in China. “Once microdramas took off, there was a nonstop stream of roles I could take on as long as I wanted to film,” said Bi Zhiqiang, 27, another actor living in Hengdian, who quickly built a career after moving there in 2021 as the industry was taking shape. “Many people who didn’t even study acting or film and television joined because there were more and more opportunities.” The lure drew thousands of crews to Hengdian last year to shoot projects in and around the sprawling Hengdian World Studios. It was a fresh injection of energy for the town and its decades-old eponymous studio, known for its large-scale replicas of some of China’s iconic imperial architecture, like the Summer Palace and the Forbidden City, and for birthing Chinese blockbusters. Other hubs — like Qingdao, Xi’an, and Zhengzhou — emerged across the country, too, with microdrama crews shooting in expressly built complexes with fake mansions, boardrooms, and ERs. But the industry quickly became a pressure cooker for actors and production crews, due to a hyper-competitive model built around cranking out as many microdramas as possible in the hopes that one would go viral. Actors and crew describe standard 18 to 20-hour working days as productions rushed to stay within budget while shooting what are essentially feature-length movies in the space of roughly a week. “As long as they keep filming, they can keep releasing. And the logic is — there will always be one that becomes a hit,” said Guo Ertai, a director and actor at the National Theater of China in Beijing, who followed audiences and money into the microdrama industry several years ago. At the bottom of the pecking order are extras, who might work long shifts for as little as 10 Chinese yuan ($1.50) per hour, a wage one former actor commented wryly was less than the rental rate for some of the animals used in productions. Even still, the allure of success kept the industry flush with young, ambitious actors, directors and creatives. Unlike film, which has a high barrier to entry, microdramas “gave an ordinary person an opportunity,” said Guo, the director. The thinking is “‘I can become rich overnight, I can become a star overnight, I can earn a lot of money overnight with very little outlay,’” he said. Microdrama actors have become celebrities in their own right with millions of followers on social media platforms. Some television and film stars — including martial arts legend Jet Li — have starred in microdramas. Even those without broad name recognition, who were able to land leading roles in successful dramas, could make multiples of an average monthly urban wage. But as more money and bigger names entered, competition grew fiercer, pushing a drive to export the dramas overseas for more revenue — and use whatever means available to cut costs. Enter AI It took a few weeks for actor Zhuang Wenjie, 28, to realize something was wrong when she returned to Hengdian after celebrating the Chinese New Year holiday in her hometown in February. She had moved to the area last summer and felt she was just beginning to make a name for herself and could start auditioning for higher profile roles. At first, she didn’t quite connect the empty streets around her with the growing number of AI-generated microdramas she saw on her social media feeds. Soon, though, it became obvious: people weren’t returning because jobs had dried up. “Suddenly (there was) a feeling of impending crisis,” Zhuang said. ByteDance’s SeeDance 2.0 had arrived. Seemingly overnight, Chinese social media was swamped with realistic-looking, AI-generated videos, as users played around with the new, powerful video generation tool. And when it came to microdramas, SeeDance 2.0 was well positioned. ByteDance owns two of the main platforms in China that host microdramas: Douyin, Tiktok’s sister app, and Hongguo. It also has a repository of novels that make up a well of copyrighted material for scripts that collaborating production teams can draw from. Other tech firms have released rival video-generating technology in recent months, including another short video app owner Kuaishuo, tech giant Alibaba and AI firm MiniMax. Using next-gen AI video tools, a 120-minute project of ordinary quality can take a five-member team roughly a week to produce and cost some 15,000 yuan, about $2,200, one production firm told CNN — less than a tenth of what’s typically cited as the low-end cost of a live production. In the first half of the year on Douyin alone, 220,000 new AI-generated microdramas racked up a staggering 500 billion views, according to DataEye, the market research firm. Some were animations, but more than half since March used AI that simulated real people. Zhuang decided to leave town in April, joining an exodus of actors and crew from the area. “The number of jobs in Hengdian was decreasing day by day, and the pay was also getting lower and lower every day … the hardship really did defeat me,” she said. Actors who did stay on described cratering salaries, such as being offered 300 yuan (about $45) a day to play the kind of leading role that would have previously paid thousands. Some have turned to side jobs to make ends meet. Liu Yuzhan, 29, says he’d been making steady money booking four new roles a month in the past couple years. Now, Liu says he’s picking up extra work as a food delivery driver. “I have my own mortgage and I’m responsible for my parents’ retirement. Given the current market of microdramas… it’s simply not enough to cover my daily expenses,” he said. The ‘bubble’ As AI tools put microdrama actors out of work, social media chat groups that used to advertise acting opportunities were swamped with a different kind of classified: for AI editors, programmers, designers and screenwriters. And a new crop of companies, editors and entrepreneurs have poured into the space. Among them is Tan Chen, a 21-year-old college student who founded a startup that began focusing on AI production in April. His team, which is based in Jinan, a provincial capital in eastern China, takes scripts or novels, and “optimizes” them for microdramas by crunching down the narratives and ramping up the excitement and suspense. They decide the look of the characters and the set, a process Tan describes as “similar to casting and location scouting,” and then build a storyboard. “We need to transform what we see in words into something that can be expressed visually. That really tests our production staff’s directorial thinking and audiovisual language abilities,” he said. How well the AI images come together depends on that language. Employees known as “card-pullers” must use prompts — typically written with the help of AI — to repeatedly generate AI video clips until they get ones that best convey the scene, which are then edited together. When his team started, Tan said clients would pay them 1,000 yuan, about $150, a minute, typically for a 120-minute project. But just like actors and live production crews, these creatives are also feeling the squeeze. A crush of programmers joined the industry and middlemen taking a cut to link creators with clients have multiplied, driving down profits for teams like Tan’s. He’s now fielding projects for as low as 150 yuan per minute — around $20. “This rapidly growing market inevitably has a certain degree of bubble,” he said. His company also recently switched to making AI-generated cartoons to avoid inadvertently using AI images that draw from real actor’s faces. ‘If you can’t beat it’ The use of AI characters that resemble real-life actors, without permission, has become a key issue in the industry — with at least one case of a well-known actor receiving court-ordered compensation, state media reports. But other actors, aren’t so lucky. Actor Yu Shutian, 31, recently found what she believes was her own face “blended into AI,” after fans alerted her to an AI-generated character that resembled her. She knew it was nearly impossible to prove the likeness was based on her face, so she never pursued legal action. She also says she realized it was probably the technology, not the creator who was responsible. “AI is unstoppable. If you can’t beat it, join it, so I’d rather find a reasonable way to embrace AI,” said Yu, who is starting to use the tech as she’s moved some of her focus to directing. That sentiment illustrates a central tension raised by many of the actors who shared their stories with CNN. While AI may render the miles of studio space and life-sized sets of places like Hengdian unnecessary, what role humans — including actors — ultimately play in the industry, working alongside AI to create art and entertainment, is far from settled, they say. Microdrama streaming app Hongguo in recent weeks raised production standards around AI-generated dramas, and ratings in recent weeks suggest there’s still viewer appetite for “real people dramas,” which rank in the platform’s top 10 alongside AI productions and cartoons. “AI is formulaic — it can’t express the full range of human emotions and desires,” said Junlin, the actor who is staying put, for now, in Hengdian. “How could it possibly replace humans?” But when it comes to the transformation underway in her industry, she sees the newer actors like herself, who are still trying to make it, as the most vulnerable. “AI absolutely can’t replace a real person,” she said. “But it might be able to replace me.”

articles.title: Northamptoshire Dogfather set for Strictly after stroke recovery
articles.summary: Graeme Hall from the Channel 5 series 'Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly' is joining Strictly Come Dancing.
articles.body:
TV dog trainer Graeme Hall says it is a "dream come true" to be on Strictly Come Dancing, after a stroke made him think he would never dance again.

The Brackley-based Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly star will appear on the BBC One show when it launches in September, despite giving up dancing after falling ill in 2019.

Known as the Dogfather on the Channel 5 television series, Hall has previously danced in local competitions, including Strictly Northampton.

"There are not a lot of people in the world that have had the chance to do this. So I'm just going to love every minute, enjoy it for what it is and hope it keeps going as long as possible," he said.

Speaking to Bernie Keith on BBC Radio Northampton , Hall said he did not expect to dance again after having a stroke caused by a hole in the heart.

"I never got back to dancing, I just thought, 'well that was a bit of fun'... and that was that.

"I put the dance bag in the loft. It's been with me through three house moves," he added.

Now having made a full recovery, Hall has dusted off his dancing kit and is "loving the experience".

Hall will only find out who his dance partner is during the launch show on 26 September 2026.

He said: "The celebrities are all really nice people, it's going to be great but it's not going to be easy because they actually, as far as I can tell, are quite good at dancing."

Hall is also known for fronting The Dog Hospital and his contributions to BBC radio programmes, ITV's This Morning, and writing a regular column for the Times.

He has written books including The Ultimate Kid's Guide to Dogs and previously made a cameo appearance in the hit drama All Creatures Great and Small.

articles.title: ‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
articles.summary: From father searching for his daughter’s body to man who drowned trying to save a friend, floods take devastating toll.
articles.body:
Assam, India – Debiram Panika, a 37-year-old daily wage labourer from northeastern India’s Assam state, would speak to his wife and two daughters on video calls every day from Dimapur, a town in neighbouring Nagaland state where he worked.

But when his phone rang at about 11am on July 19, there was panic in the voice of his 30-year-old wife, Dipika.

“I could only see my wife telling me on the video call, ‘This is it for us. We are going to die,’ before the call was disconnected,” Panika recalled, speaking to Al Jazeera.

It was the last time they spoke. Moments later, rising waters from the nearby Dikhow River, which snakes past their village in Assam’s Sivasagar district, surged into their bamboo-and-mud home with a ferocious current and swept away Dipika and four-year-old daughter Radhika.

“The water came flooding like sea waves, and they were gone in a flash,” Panika said, as he stood in front of the ruined home he has since returned to.

Sivasagar is part of the eastern Assam region, also referred to as Upper Assam. Incessant rains between July 18 and July 20 submerged the region and the neighbouring Naga Hills of Nagaland.

Monsoon floods usually impact northern and western Assam, and parts of central Assam, the worst. But several Nagaland districts bordering Upper Assam received heavy rainfall on those three days, leading to dozens of landslides. This intense run-off swelled Naga Hills-origin rivers and caused devastation downstream.

The resultant floods killed more than 100 people, destroyed 2,700 villages, and displaced 700,000 people across the state. The state government says 1.2 million people were impacted in all, their lives disrupted.

Most waters have since receded, but Radhika’s body is yet to be found.

“I look for Radhika every day in the bushes, tirelessly,” Panika said, holding back his tears. “Her last words, calling me ‘Papa’, are still reverberating in my ears.”

Panika’s other daughter, Ridhika, 10, was at a relative’s place a few metres away when her mother and sister were swept away by the flood. Ridhika held onto a bamboo bush and was later rescued by locals.

Several riverine villages in Sivasagar have been wrecked by debris carried down by the waters of the Dikhow from the surrounding Naga Hills.

Tens of thousands of tree trunks lie piled up in places that used to be homes, as lush rice fields, the main source of livelihood, have been washed away.

Kukil Das, a 30-year-old Facebook vlogger in Debiram’s village of Nepali Khuti, told Al Jazeera that “the torrent of the flood was like an apocalyptic event seen in the movies.

“Trees as tall as 30 to 40 metres (100-130ft) came down from the hills, flooding the river, and wiped out everything as they crashed against our homes,” he said. “There is no home left. It was a tsunami.”

Das and his friend Shravan Prasad, from the neighbouring Bihubor village, said they saved at least 1,000 lives by using boats the two villages had at that time.

“We put together a group of friends with the seven boats and started rescuing people turn by turn for two days and nights without food and water,” Prasad said.

Das said the floods forced residents to take shelter on the roofs of concrete homes they could find, as cries for help and the sounds of the river washing away homes echoed in the neighbourhood.

Laxmi Sharma, who owned one such concrete house, said she provided shelter to at least 60 people on her terrace after the river water gushed into Nepali Khuti.

“People ran towards the roof of my building. We thought we were going to die,” Sharma, 46, told Al Jazeera. “But it is a miracle that we are still alive even though my house was barely out of water.”

Not everyone could escape the flood’s wrath, though.

In Sivasagar’s Simaluguri village, two friends – Reihana Ahmed, a Muslim, and Ratul Swarna, a Hindu, both in their 30s – were swept away in the torrent.

When Ahmed, a mother of two, was drowning as the deluge entered her village, Swarna, who did not know how to swim, jumped to save her without thinking about his life.

The two friends were later found dead in the paddy fields. “It was humanity that won in a disaster like this,” Ahmed’s husband Aminul Haque said with a sorrowful smile.

Besides the eroding banks of the Dikhow River in Prajabasti, another flood-affected village, 75-year-old Asor Ali sat in disbelief next to his wife, Jamila Khatun.

“Even the generations preceding me have not seen a flood like this,” he said, staring at the flowing river. “Even the 1950s earthquake that triggered the floods here did not do so much damage.”

A magnitude 8.6 earthquake hit Assam and Tibet across the border in 1950, altering the region’s riverine system. Nearly 5,000 people died. Since then, Assam has witnessed frequent floods, which intensify during the monsoons, says Mirza Zulfiqur Rahman, a researcher on the basin of the Brahmaputra, the region’s major river: The Naga Hills rivers that flooded Upper Assam are its tributaries.

But residents say this year’s deadly deluge is not just a natural phenomenon.

Biren Gogoi, 43, says rampant stone and sand mining in regional rivers, coupled with aggressive deforestation and coal extraction in Nagaland’s Mon district, triggered the devastation.

Global Nature Watch, an open-source online platform that provides real-time data on deforestation across the world, showed that Nagaland lost 14 percent of its tree cover between 2002 and 2025, with Mon district bordering Assam’s Sivasagar being the most affected.

According to the latest report published in 2023 by the Forest Survey of India, Nagaland has lost about 794.88 square kilometres (306.9 square miles) of forest cover between 2013 and 2023.

Al Jazeera travelled along the Assam-Nagaland border and saw signs of deforestation on the hills and mining activities in both the states. Satellite images also confirmed rampant coal mining in Nagaland’s Mon district, and stone mining crushers on Assam’s side, especially in Bihubor, one of the epicentres of the Assam flood.

While Mon’s Deputy Commissioner Wennyei Konyak acknowledged the possibility of illegal mining in the district, he added that the land was protected under Indian laws to uphold the rights of Indigenous tribes, and therefore government interference in the area was limited.

“I would not blame mining activities for the flood. It was just the wrath of nature,” he told Al Jazeera.

But experts and political leaders in Assam say mining played a direct role in the floods.

Debabrata Saikia of the opposition Congress party, who is a former legislator from Sivasagar constituency, accused Assam’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of allowing illegal excavations for stone and sand on the Dikhow riverbank, resulting in a cratered wasteland that worsened the floods.

“This unchecked plundering of riverbeds and hills under the ruling government has engineered this into a man-made disaster,” Saikia told Al Jazeera.

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, however, rejected the allegation on August 4, blaming excessive rainfall in Nagaland for triggering the Upper Assam deluge. On August 14, Ranoj Pegu, a cabinet minister in the state’s BJP government, blamed erratic rainfall due to climate change for the deluge.

Rahman, the Brahmaputra river basin researcher, believes that while the climate crisis played a role, the flood was “purely human-made”, caused by the fracturing of the landscape.

“The unrestrained stone extraction from the Dikhow riverbed has damaged the river’s natural cushion,” Rahman said. “That means the river loses the capacity to resist high flows of torrents that break embankments and cause floods.”

An official document from 2022, seen by Al Jazeera, also highlights mining as a factor in possible large-scale floods downstream on the Assam side.

Al Jazeera reached out to senior district officials in Sivasagar as well as state government officials for their comments on allegations of unchecked coal mining but did not get any response.

Back in Prajabasti village, Ali, the septuagenarian, is mentally preparing himself for future floods.

“It will happen again, so long as there is greed for land and coal in humans,” he said. “Nature pays them back.”

articles.title: China’s new moon mission could unlock secret of lunar ice: Why that matters
articles.summary: The Chang’e-7 seeks to find out more about the water trapped within the moon’s shadowed craters.
articles.body:
China is set to launch its Chang’e-7 unmanned, robotic space mission, possibly as early as Monday morning, to look for ice water in the permanently shadowed craters of the moon’s south pole.

This marks China’s seventh and most ambitious moon mission so far. Here is what we know about it.

The Chang’e‑7 launch window runs from Monday, August 24 to Monday, August 31, according to launch observers. That means the mission could lift off on any day in that period.

The Chang’e-7 comprises an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper.

The orbiter is the main spacecraft which will remain in the moon’s orbit, mapping the surface and taking images while the mission is under way. It will also relay data and communications between the other Chang’e‑7 components and Earth.

The lander is the vessel that will touch down on the lunar surface, loaded with the necessary scientific instruments for lunar exploration, near the edge of the Shackleton Crater, a 21km-wide (13-mile-wide) pit close to the moon’s south pole. Lunar missions before this have never come this close to the pole.

The rover is a small robotic vehicle which can drive around the landing site and which carries equipment to analyse the local environment, including rocks and soil.

The hopper is a small robotic craft powered by solar energy, designed to “hop” – or fly – short distances from the surface of the moon and land again. It will be used to explore the Shackleton Crater.

How do we know there is water on the moon?

Over the past two decades, several space missions have established that there is water on the moon.

Since the 1960s, even before the first Apollo landing in 1969, scientists speculated that water could exist on the moon. However, when Apollo crews returned samples for testing in the late 1960s and early 1970s, they appeared to be dry.

Finally, in 2009, NASA deliberately crashed a rocket segment and its probe into a shadowed lunar crater to analyse the dust plume it kicked up. This provided one of the clearest direct confirmations that significant ice water does exist on the moon, building on earlier detections of water and hydrogen by probes.

In October 2020, NASA scientists announced that water on the moon is more widespread than previously known. They said water molecules had been found to be encapsulated within mineral grains on the lunar surface and speculated that more water is hidden in ice patches which are in permanent shadows.

NASA describes these permanent shadows as dark areas inside deep craters near the north and south poles of the moon where sunlight has not reached for millions or even billions of years. In 2018, prior to confirming it in 2020, NASA had detected water ice in shadowed parts of the moon through mapping.

Why is it important to find out more about the water on the moon?

Expanding knowledge about water on the moon is vital because ancient polar ice may have preserved a record of lunar volcanic activity and of water delivered by comets and asteroids to the Earth-moon system, offering clues to how our own oceans originally formed.

Additionally, if there is enough water on the moon that is realistically accessible, it could serve as a source of drinking water for crewed lunar missions, and could also help to keep equipment cool.

Hydrogen could also be extracted from moon water to provide fuel, while oxygen could be extracted to breathe, supporting onward missions to Mars or lunar mining.

Could anyone ‘own’ the water on the moon?

The 1967 United Nations Outer Space Treaty bans any nation from claiming sovereignty over the moon or owning it as territory. It does not explicitly prohibit commercial operations, but it requires private activities in space to be authorised and supervised by states and leaves key questions about resource ownership unresolved.

Which recent space missions have searched for frozen water on the moon?

In 2023, Russia’s lunar spacecraft , Luna-25, was launched to look for frozen water in the moon’s south pole. However, the Luna-25 spun out of control and crashed. The crash prevented any scientific data collection or water discovery.

Racing against the Luna-25 mission was India’s Chandrayaan-3, which also aimed to expand knowledge of lunar water ice. Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed in August 2023 and found critical new evidence of water on the surface of the moon’s south pole through soil temperature readings.

Why is exploring the moon’s south pole a challenge?

Attempted landings at the moon’s south pole have failed before because of its challenging terrain, which is full of craters and deep trenches.

The south pole is far from the equatorial region targeted by previous missions, including the crewed Apollo landings.

What is different about the Chang’e-7 mission?

The upcoming Chang’e-7 is aiming to expand knowledge about where, exactly, water is located in the craters of the moon, how deep it is, what form it is in and whether it is indeed possible to access it.

The Chang’e-7’s six-legged hopper has been designed to jump into and out of the deep, shadowed craters near the south pole that are hard for traditional rovers to reach, to look for water ice and other resources.

No previous space mission has used a dedicated hopper to jump in and out of lunar craters in this way.

articles.title: Make a Difference Awards NI: Belfast 'hidden gem' among finalists
articles.summary: Annadale Community Garden Group is one of four groups or individuals in the running for this year's Make a Difference Awards NI.
articles.body:
From a lifeless strip of grass to a blossoming garden, Annadale Community Centre's grounds have received a glow up over the past year, becoming a "hidden gem" for all to enjoy.

The volunteer group has now been recognised for its contribution to the local area, receiving a nomination for the BBC Make a Difference Awards .

Annadale Community Centre Gardening Group meets every Tuesday and will celebrate its first birthday in September.

Residents say the space has not only improved the local environment but has also created a welcoming community hub where people can learn new skills, share ideas and support each other through life's challenges.

Kirstie Rowan has been involved since the beginning and is proud of the journey the group has been on, which has been full of "lovely big changes".

"We started with the grass, unwanted containers and the polytunnel and now we have all of this â we've got the pond, tree bed and vegetables as well," she explained.

"Every week when we come down there's always more growth, more flowers, new flowers, it really is beautiful.

"Some of us don't work so this gets us out of the house weekly and even if we come, we aren't expected to do anything, its just nice to be here with everyone."

For Fayth Duffy, being part of the group has been a "game changer" for her after recently moving to the area.

"I was really finding it hard to put down roots and meet friends because when your kids get a bit older you're not meeting the mums at the gate, you're not getting out to the other places such as toddler groups," she said.

"We've all become such good friends, we go for coffee together sometimes afterwards and support each other, we'll ring each other to make sure we are all here."

For local resident Larry Andrews the group has been a refuge following the death of his wife last year.

"I came here for a bit of company, my daughter found it on WhatsApp and I've been coming since September last year," he said.

The 87-year-old former butcher has made new friends through the group.

"It's good to meet different people and have a yarn with themâ¦ It's amazing the number of people you do find," he added.

Amber Jennings works with the group and is on hand with gardening tips and advice.

"It means a lot to be nominated for this award - I feel like this is such a hidden gem on the Ormeau Road for people to retreat to on a Tuesday morning and learn how to garden with those in the community," she said.

The primary goal of the group is to "improve the wellbeing of people in the area".

Jennings has seen first hand the difference the garden has made to members.

"It's been a really uplifting experience for all involved, having that routine, knowing you're outside and being with people in your community," she added.

It is awarded to an individual or group who improve or conserve their local environment.

Annadale Community Centre Garden Group is one of four finalists in the category, along with:

Daniel McAfee - Ballycastle, a wildlife volunteer and member of the Glens Red Squirrel Group where he shares his knowledge through school visits, talks and guided nature walks

Alannah Agnew - Cookstown , a passionate member and chairperson of her school eco team. She has led assemblies on climate change, littering and healthy eating, while helping her school achieve its sixth Green Flag award

Eco Rangers NI - Carrickfergus, a community litter-picking group that clears litter year-round, supports community events and helps young people with awards such as the Duke of Edinburgh Award

Overall winners will be announced live on Vinny and Cate's BBC Radio Ulster show on Friday 25 September.

articles.title: Residents in China found three king cobra nests; scientists saw two cobras guarding one with 72 eggs
articles.summary: China News: Three king cobra nests discovered by residents in Yunnan, China, have given scientists an unusually close look at a part of the snakeâs life that rema.
articles.body: Three king cobra nests discovered by residents in Yunnan, China, have given scientists an unusually close look at a part of the snakeâs life that remains poorly documented. The nests, found between 2020 and 2025 in different parts of the province, contained 30, 72 and 25 eggs. The largest clutch, found west of Kunming, was particularly unexpected, with two king cobras observed guarding the same nest during several visits. Scientists could not establish the snakesâ sexes, leaving open the possibility that two females had contributed to the unusually large clutch. The other nests were found in bamboo forests, including one where young king cobras were later seen emerging. The observations are significant because they represent the first documented king cobra nesting and clutch-size records in China outside the Xizang Autonomous Region. The findings also add to growing evidence that the speciesâ nesting behaviour may be more varied than previously recorded. The observations are especially valuable because king cobras are difficult to study in the wild, and their reproductive behaviour is still not fully understood. By documenting nest locations, egg numbers and parental behaviour, the findings provide rare details that can help researchers better understand how the species reproduces in different environments.Two king cobras guarded a nest near Kunming in 2024According to the study published in Integrative Conservation, titled âNovel Natural History Observations on the Reproductive Biology of King Cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) From Yunnan Province, Chinaâ, the first nest was found on 10 July 2020 in Menghai County, in Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture in southern Yunnan. Local residents came across it in a tropical bamboo forest at an elevation of about 1,730 metres. The nest was made largely from bamboo leaves and an adult king cobra was guarding it, believed by the researchers to be a female.Once the snake had moved away, the nest could be examined. Inside were 30 eggs, with developing embryos visible when the eggs were illuminated with a strong light. The observation was important because, before these records, documented information about king cobra nesting in China was largely confined to southeastern Xizang. The authors describe the three Yunnan observations as the first documented nesting and clutch-size records for the species in China outside that region.The second discovery was made several years later, on 6 June 2024, in a mixed forest west of Kunming. This time, residents found two king cobras at a nest made from pine needles. The snakes were still there when researchers returned on 1 July, with one measuring about 1.8 metres and the other more than 2 metres long.The nest itself was changing as the snakes continued working on it. By the July survey, it stood roughly 1 metre high and measured around 1.5 metres across. The researchers later found 72 eggs packed towards the centre of the structure. The eggs sat roughly half a metre above the ground and below the upper layer of nesting material. Temperatures inside the nest were estimated at between 35Â°C and 40Â°C, considerably warmer than the surrounding air.Scientists find new evidence of group guarding in king cobrasThe Kunming nest was unusual for another reason. Two king cobras were seen guarding it during the early observations, and both remained at the site during a second survey on 11 July. By 20 July, however, only the larger snake was still there. It eventually left the nest without incident when the researchers approached.The observation matters because the question of whether several king cobras can participate in guarding the same nest has remained uncertain. Older accounts had described both sexes taking part in nest guarding, but more recent field studies had not confirmed this behaviour. The authors say the Kunming observation provides new evidence that multiple individuals can participate in guarding a king cobra nest. They could not determine the sex of either snake, so the observation does not establish exactly how the two individuals were related or what role each played.The unusually large clutch found there made the situation even harder to explain. King cobra clutches reported in earlier studies have generally ranged from 14 to 37 eggs. Seventy-two eggs is far beyond that range and, according to the authors, is the largest clutch reported in published studies of Ophiophagus hannah in the strict sense.There are a couple of possibilities. The nest could have belonged to a single mating pair, with one female producing an exceptionally large clutch. The researchers also raise another explanation: two females may have nested together, combining their eggs in one nest. The fact that the 72 eggs were roughly twice the size of clutches recorded elsewhere lends some support to that idea, but the researchers stress that they could not determine the snakes' sexes. It remains a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.King cobra nest in Yunnan contained 25 eggsThe third nest was found in Lancang County, Pu'er City, south-central Yunnan, on 17 June 2025. Residents again made the initial discovery. They reported seeing two adult king cobras guarding the nest, although only one was present when the researchers visited.This nest was smaller than the one near Kunming. It had been built in a bamboo forest from bamboo leaves and twigs, measuring about 95 centimetres across at its base and roughly 50 centimetres high. Once the guarding snake left, researchers found 25 eggs inside, joined together as a single cluster. The temperature within the nest was about 26Â°C, the same as the surrounding air.The nest also offered something the other observations did not: a chance to see what happened after the eggs were laid. Juvenile king cobras were first observed emerging from the nest on 19 August 2025. That gave the researchers a direct record connecting the nesting site with successful hatching, adding another piece to an otherwise limited picture of reproduction in the species.The 25-egg clutch also sits comfortably within the range of previously recorded king cobra clutches. That makes the 72-egg Kunming nest stand out even more. Taken together, the three nests contained 30, 72 and 25 eggs, showing how much clutch size can vary between individual nesting events.King cobra nesting records help fill a geographical gap in ChinaKing cobras are unusual among snakes because they construct nests and guard their eggs. Yet despite being one of the world's best-known venomous snakes, their reproductive biology is still poorly documented across much of their range.The study notes that earlier work has been concentrated largely in the eastern Himalaya, where recorded clutches have ranged from 14 to 37 eggs. In China, the previous official nesting record came from southeastern Xizang. The Yunnan observations therefore fill an important geographical gap, particularly because they cover three separate nesting events in different parts of the province.The findings also need to be viewed in light of changes in how the species itself is classified. What was once treated as a single widespread king cobra species has more recently been considered a species complex containing four distinct species. The Ophiophagus hannah species in the study is now understood to occur in the Pan-Himalayan region, southern China and much of Indochina. It is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN and as Endangered on China's Red List.For the researchers, the value of the Yunnan records is therefore not simply the discovery of three nests. The observations provide baseline information that can be compared with nesting behaviour elsewhere and may help determine whether the apparent group guarding and unusually large clutch in Kunming are rare exceptions or signs of behaviour that has simply gone undocumented.The authors say further fieldwork will be needed to test the competing explanations for the 72-egg nest. Whether it was produced by one unusually productive female or resulted from two females nesting together cannot be resolved from the observations available.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sri Lankan cricket legend Kumar Sangakkara spent years restoring a historic villa built more than 100 years ago, blending old-world architecture with modern design; the heritage property is now ready for a new chapter
articles.summary: Kumar Sangakkara is a name that needs no introduction. Everyone who follows cricket or even who doesnât, knows the Sri Lankan cricket legend. But what.
articles.body: Kumar Sangakkara is a name that needs no introduction. Everyone who follows cricket or even who doesnât, knows the Sri Lankan cricket legend. But what people donât know is that back in 2008, Kumar Sangakkara along with his wife Yehali bought a house inside Galle Fort, also known as the Dutch Fort or the "Ramparts of Galle". The couple were already in love with its scenic coastal location, but were not aware of what was inside the fort. When they bought the 120-year old villa, their first look came with an unpleasant surprise because it was in such poor condition.But 20 years later, the property has emerged as an unusual meeting point of Sri Lankaâs history and modern design. Itâs a restoration that recently took the world by surprise after featuring by ABC Australiaâs Culture by Design.However, for travellers the story is about more than a famous cricketerâs beautiful home. It offers a glimpse into why Galle Fort is among Sri Lankaâs most fascinating heritage destinations. Why restoring a historic building is very different from simply renovating an old house.Letâs find out more about the iconic propertyA home inside one of Asiaâs great fortified citiesGalle Fort is set on Sri Lankaâs southwestern coast. It has also been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988. UNESCO describes the Old Town of Galle and its fortifications as an outstanding example of a European-built fortified city in South and Southeast Asia.The story of the fort goes back to the 16th century. It was the time the Portuguese established the fortified settlement, and under Dutch rule in the 17th and 18th centuries, the fort developed into the remarkable place that visitors see today. Later British influence added another layer to the region.This incredible mix is exactly what makes walking through Galle Fort so atmospheric. Narrow streets, verandas, courtyards, old houses, churches, warehouses and massive ramparts sit alongside cafÃ©s, galleries, shops and homes.Sri Lanka Tourism describes Galle Fort as a historical, archaeological and architectural monument with 14 major bastions, while UNESCO highlights its distinctive street grid, courtyards, verandas and even a 17th-century underground drainage system that remains in use.Sangakkaraâs dreamFor Sangakkara and Yehali, the main challenge was to retain the fortâs old look without stripping off its identity. They called in architects Jeevan D'Souza and Murad Ismail and interior designer Annika Fernando to make their dream into reality. Rather than treating the historic fabric as something that needed to be hidden behind freshly finished surfaces, the team chose to make much of it part of the design.Some of the villa's old coral construction was deliberately left exposed including weathered walls and layers of patina. Talking to ABC, Fernando said that the contrast between aged surfaces and clean new finishes eventually became an important part of the home's character.A unique design challengeOne of the most memorable details from the restoration involves a huge sculpture by Sri Lankan artist Prageeth Manohansa.The sculpture was intended to become a centrepiece of the home, but there was a problem: it was too big to pass through any of the doors. But the problemâs solution was wonderfully unconventional. The artwork was brought into the house before the restoration began, and the building was then renovated around it.It is a small detail, but it captures the philosophy behind the project. Instead of forcing the historic house to conform completely to modern requirements, the designers repeatedly worked around what was already there.From damaged villa to modern family homeToday, itâs a four-bedroom residence with three courtyard gardens and a rooftop swimming pool overlooking the historic surroundings, including views towards Galle Lighthouse. Rooms combine contemporary interiors with artworks, antiques and surviving elements of the original building.Sangakkara described the house as a reflection of how new residents coexist with an old community. That idea matters in Galle Fort, which is not merely an archaeological site but a living historic urban area. UNESCO's current conservation guidance specifically encourages restoration and adaptive reuse while stressing the importance of retaining historically authentic building fabric.Galle Fort, a must-visit attraction in Sri LankaFor travellers, Sangakkara's villa is a reminder to look beyond the postcard views of Galle Fort.Walk along the ramparts around sunset, explore the narrow lanes, notice the old verandas and courtyards, visit the historic churches and museums, and look closely at how different architectural traditions overlap.It is the country's one of the most distinctive attractions, while UNESCO's World Heritage designation rests on precisely this unusual interaction between European architecture and South Asian traditions.Sangakkara's restoration adds another chapter to that story. His villa demonstrates that conservation does not necessarily mean turning a historic building into a relic. Sometimes, the best way to preserve a building is to give it another lifeâcarefully, respectfully and without hiding the marks of time.Inside this particular Galle Fort house, the old still live, the courtyards have been revived and modern life has moved in but the old is gold character can still be felt. The cricket legend may have traded the stadium for a heritage villa, but his most interesting Galle project is ultimately a lesson in travel itself.For visitors, it also offers a different way to experience heritage: not simply by photographing old walls, but by understanding the stories, craftsmanship and lives that continue to shape them today. For anyone planning a trip to Sri Lanka, Galle Fort is therefore worth experiencing slowly rather than treating it as a quick sightseeing stop. Its real charm lies in the details. An old doorway, a weathered wall, a shaded courtyard or a house that has been given a new purpose without losing its pastSources: ABC Australiaâs Culture by Design; UNESCO World Heritage Centre; Sri Lanka Tourism; UNESCO state-of-conservation and heritage documentation.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: 'Repeatedly tortured': Imran Khan's sister alleges abuse in jail as ex-Pakistan PM returns to prison
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan's jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she said on Saturday, a day after .
articles.body: Pakistan's jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she said on Saturday, a day after he was taken to a state-run hospital for a brief medical examination and sent back to jail.Khan's sister, Uzma Khan, attended his examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad and said the former prime minister was physically fit but had repeatedly complained of torture.âKhan told me that he is being repeatedly tortured in prisonâ, she told the media.The interior and law ministries, along with jail authorities, have not responded to a Reuters request for comment on the allegation.Khan was taken to PIMS overnight on Friday after the Supreme Court had directed authorities to transfer him from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for a medical examination. He was declared medically fit and returned to prison within hours.PTI files contempt petitionKhan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party on Saturday filed a contempt petition against the government, accusing authorities of violating the Supreme Court's order by taking him to PIMS instead of the private hospital named by the court.The petition seeks action against senior government officials and asks that Khan be taken to Shifa International Hospital for treatment, PTI legal adviser Naeem Panjutha said."The petition seeks action against the âprime minister, law minister, information minister" and other government officials, Panjutha said, adding that it also calls for Khan's treatment at the private hospital ordered by the court.The PTI also alleged that Khan was denied access to his personal physician, which it said amounted to another breach of the Supreme Court's directive.A three-judge Supreme Court bench had on Tuesday directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital within two days for a medical examination.The PTI interprets the order as requiring Khan to remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September.Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the decision to take Khan to PIMS instead of the court-named private hospital was made because of security concerns.Khan declared medically fit, sent back to jailKhan was examined by a team of doctors, including an ophthalmologist, cardiologist and physician, before being declared medically fit and sent back to Adiala jail in Rawalpindi."A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist and a physician conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit," Tarar said.Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 and maintains that the cases against him are politically motivated. The government denies the allegation.His lawyers have previously said his health has deteriorated in prison and that he has suffered substantial loss of vision in his right eye. The government has maintained that medical reports have found no condition requiring immediate treatment.Supporters gather after brief hospital visitKhan's supporters gathered along roads in Islamabad overnight, throwing flowers at a vehicle believed to be carrying him to the hospital.The scenes were broadcast live on Pakistani television, in a notable departure from recent years when broadcasters often avoided mentioning Khan's name.PTI leaders have warned that the latest developments could increase pressure on the government and fuel fresh demonstrations."After what happened yesterday, the pressure (on authorities) will double," Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said, adding that preparations for a protest march planned for September 27 had picked up.Khan's arrest and imprisonment have remained a major source of political tension in Pakistan. His arrest in 2023 triggered widespread protests, including attacks on military installations, and his supporters continue to demand his release.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sydney Marathon medal wrongly features Munich stadium
articles.summary: Online sleuths detected the error after Sydney Marathon unveiled the double-sided medal.
articles.body:
One week out from the world-renowned Sydney Marathon, organisers face questions about whether designers etched the wrong city's stadium on the participation medal.

The medal appears to feature a stadium carved in the likeness of Allianz Arena in the German city of Munich, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney – which the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course runs past.

The BBC has reached out to Sydney Marathon for comment.

Some 40,000 runners will be taking part in the event on 30 August, after more than 120,000 ballot entries.

Speculation about a possible mix-up began after Sydney Marathon's official social media account unveiled its design for the 2026 medal, inviting users to "look closely and you'll find the story of the course in the details".

They continued: "A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way - starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House."

Munich's Allianz Arena is sculpted by thousands of diamond-shaped inflatable cushions, while Sydney's similarly-named Allianz Stadium has a flatter façade smoothed with long bronze fins.

The other face of the double-sided medal features a gold and indigo pattern designed by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian. Forty-two half-round markings lining the circular edge "represent each kilometre of the course", organisers explained.

Killian told the BBC he was not responsible for the other artwork.

The blunder follows a similar incident at last year's Great North Run in Newcastle, where medals mistakenly featured the Sunderland and Wear River – which is not part of the event.

Sydney was announced as the seventh city added to the Abbott majors series in 2024, joining London, Berlin, Boston, Chicago, New York, and Tokyo. Cape Town is set to become the eighth city when it hosts its first marathon major next year.

articles.title: Spain’s ‘wolf boy of Sierra Morena’ dies aged 80
articles.summary: For most of his childhood, Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja lived in remote Spanish mountains, isolated from human contact. He spent 12 extraordinary years being raised by wolves, after early tragedy had led to his abandonment.
articles.body: He became known as “the wolf boy of Sierra Morena.” For most of his childhood, Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja lived in these remote Spanish mountains, isolated from human contact. He spent 12 extraordinary years being raised by wolves, after early tragedy had led to his abandonment. Rodríguez eventually returned to civilization and settled in the hamlet of Rante in 2001, where he lived until his death last week, aged 80, according to the local government of San Cibrao das Viñas. “He was a person made of earth, wind, air, rain, and hunting dens,” Arturo Arcones, who knew Rodríguez in his final years, told Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE. “He always said that his happiest life was with the wolves, because he didn’t feel very comfortable with humans.” Born in 1946, in a country recovering from a civil war and a world war, Rodríguez entered a life marked by poverty in the southern Spanish village of Añora. After his mother’s death, Rodríguez’s siblings went to live with relatives while he stayed with his father, who remarried and moved the family to the Sierra Morena mountains to make charcoal, according to Professor Gabriel Janer Manila. As part of a social study, Manila spent five months interviewing Rodríguez for the philosophy department at the University of Palma de Mallorca. Pantoja was abused by his stepmother and was sold by his father to an elderly goat herder when he was just seven, public broadcaster RTVE reported. “They took me to the mountains, to a cave. A little old man with a beard came out wearing cork shoes,” Pantoja told Manila in an interview, describing an initiation into a wilderness existence. “There were howling wolves, foxes, mountain goats, deer, scorpions, snakes. At night, I heard these animals and I was afraid.” The herder cared for Pantoja, keeping him warm with animal skins, teaching him to milk the goats, and how to hunt rabbits with a stick. Under the old man’s tutelage, Pantoja learned “the law of the jungle,” Manila wrote in his study. He understood he was different – “especially because he had hands” – but still felt part of their community, Manila wrote. He mastered animal sounds, from birdsong to the cry of the deer, and believed he could communicate “effortlessly with foxes, wolves and even snakes.” When the herder disappeared unexpectedly, Pantoja drew on the skills he had learned to survive on his own and gained the trust of a wolf pack by bringing food for their cubs and howling when he sensed danger. “I was crying and they jumped up at me… then they showed me the way to their cave, the wolf’s den,” Pantoja told Manila, describing the pups playing and jumping around as they greeted him. Pantoja avoided civilization, hiding whenever he heard human voices, until the Civil Guard found him, aged 19, “lost and alone, among the ravines,” Manila wrote. “I was doing very well and I didn’t know what money was but I never lacked food,” Pantoja told RTVE news show Informe Semanal in 2010. “If I wanted to fish, I fished in the river. If I wanted a rabbit, I caught it. If I wanted a deer, I called to my parents who were the wolves. I let out a howl, I hid in the river and the wolves brought the cattle down to me.” Returning to society Those who met Pantoja during the first months of his reintegration into society recalled his intelligence of nature and his “wild character,” Manila wrote in his study. The scholar noted his “complete lack of awareness when it came to social life, his language difficulties – especially his lack of knowledge of the names of things – his strange gait, his naiveté.” After being caught by the Guardia Civil in 1965, Pantoja lived with a priest in the southern city of Jaén, and with nuns in the capital Madrid. After completing his military service he ended up in Mallorca working in hotels and restaurants, RTVE said in a 2010 report. While on the Balearic island he had a chance encounter with anthropologist Manila, who studied his journey and became the first person to believe him, RTVE said. In his later years, Pantoja dedicated himself to sharing his story, “with the intention of protecting nature and fostering a better understanding of it,” his friend Arcones told RTVE. His life continued to draw interest, with Manila publishing his doctoral thesis as a book, “I played with Wolves,” and the release of a film adaptation of his life, “Among Wolves.” Pantoja built a new life in Rante, sharing a home with a retired police officer, according to a tribute from the local government posted Monday on social media. Later, a fellow resident gave him a house, and neighbors supported him, especially during his final two years of illness. “Marcos arrived in Rante with a story that the world knew,” the tribute read. “He leaves, leaving here a story that is also ours.”

articles.title: Before Xi-Trump talks, US Navy flies through Taiwan Strait, puts China on notice
articles.summary: China News: A US Navy aircraft flew through the Taiwan Strait on Friday, putting one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relations back in focus just weeks b.
articles.body: A US Navy aircraft flew through the Taiwan Strait on Friday, putting one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relations back in focus just weeks before a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The US Navy's P-8A Poseidon aircraft transited the strait in international airspace, with the US 7th Fleet saying the operation demonstrated Washington's commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific."By operating âwithin the Taiwan Strait in accordance with international âlaw, the United States upholds the navigational rights and freedoms of all nations," the 7th Fleet said in a statement."The aircraft's transit of the Taiwan Strait demonstrates the United States' commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific. The âUnited States military flies, sails, and operates anywhere international law allows."The timing of the operation is notable as Washington and Beijing prepare for a potential Xi-Trump meeting next month, with both sides seeking to stabilise relations strained by disputes over Taiwan, trade and technology.China tracks US aircraftChina's military tracked and monitored the US aircraft throughout its transit, the state-backed Global Times reported, citing a military source who said the "situation was under control".The Taiwan Strait has long been a flashpoint between Washington and Beijing. US military ships and aircraft periodically operate through or over the waterway, moves that China strongly opposes.Beijing claims Taiwan as its territory and says it has jurisdiction over the strait. Washington and Taipei maintain that the Taiwan Strait is an international waterway and that freedom of navigation applies there.The latest US operation therefore carries a message beyond the aircraft's routine patrol role. Washington is reaffirming its interpretation of international law in a waterway that Beijing considers closely tied to its sovereignty claims.Why Taiwan matters before Xi-Trump talksThe planned meeting between Xi and Trump comes as the US and China look to prevent tensions over Taiwan, trade and technology restrictions from derailing their broader relationship.Taiwan remains among Beijing's most sensitive issues. China has repeatedly called the Taiwan question an internal affair and a core national interest, warning that it is a red line that must not be crossed.Taiwan, however, rejects China's sovereignty claims and says its future can only be decided by its people.The US does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan but maintains close unofficial ties with Taipei and is bound by US law to provide Taiwan with defensive support.Against this backdrop, the Taiwan Strait transit allows Washington to reinforce its position without directly altering its broader diplomatic engagement with Beijing.The operation also comes at a time when both sides are trying to stabilise relations. The planned Xi-Trump meeting could address disputes over trade, technology restrictions and Taiwan, making the issue particularly sensitive ahead of the talks.For Beijing, the central question remains sovereignty over Taiwan and the surrounding waters. For Washington, the issue is maintaining access to what it considers international waters.Friday's flight brought those competing positions into focus just as the two leaders prepare to sit across the table.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Screwworm is squeezing ranchers on both sides of the border
articles.summary: On Monday, the US government will reopen part of the southern border to Mexican livestock following a screwworm outbreak. It has reignited a decades-old debate in the cattle industry.
articles.body: Cattle rancher Johnny Mestas doesn’t want to get too worked up about New World screwworm, a fly whose parasitic larvae can eat cattle alive. The 74-year-old says he’s already had two heart attacks over the long course of his career farming in the parched San Luis Valley of southern Colorado. “Not everybody is meant to be a farmer,” said Mestas. “You’ve got to be half-crazy. There’s three elements you fight: the market, the weather and your neighbors.” Half-crazy or not, Mestas is uneasy about a new development in the ongoing saga of the screwworm: the US government’s plan to reopen part of the southern border to Mexican livestock on Monday. To prevent the spread of screwworm, the cattle trade with Mexico has been shuttered on and off since November 2024, with the current border closure put in place in July 2025. But next week, the border will reopen in Douglas, Arizona for cattle from Sonora, Mexico. The issue has reanimated a decades-old debate over protectionism within the cattle industry. Several US cattle producers say they are being pitted against Mexican ranchers and American meatpackers amid soaring beef prices for US consumers. Mexican producers are optimistic that the border reopening might staunch over a year of financial bleeding. Alvaro Bustillos, the head of the rancher’s union in the Mexican state of Chihuahua, hopes that a successful reopening in Sonora might lead to renewed cross-border trade with his region. The border closure nearly killed his business. “I had to fire people,” Bustillos told CNN. “It took me years to build my team. It took me years to build relationships. This is not only about the cattle trade. This is about families bonded together.” But US ranchers warn that they’re bleeding, too. One of the loudest voices in the cattle world agitating against the border reopening is Bill Bullard, the CEO of R-CALF, a national association of independent cattle and sheep farmers. Bullard, a former rancher from South Dakota, speaks about screwworm as one element of a broader crisis facing American ranchers: namely, an influx of less expensive cattle and beef from Mexico. “In just over a generation’s time, we wiped out half (of) our cattle producers in this country,” said Bullard in an interview with CNN. “It’s because we have been growing our dependence on foreign sources, displacing our domestic production in the United States. It is a threat to national security.” US officials had chosen to open the border at Sonora due to the state’s high industry standards and its lack of screwworm cases. Yet just days before, Sonora reported its first screwworm infestation, though the single case doesn’t appear to have slowed the US Department of Agriculture’s plans. The agency said Thursday that it intends to move ahead with the reopening. Even before Sonora reported its first case, many American ranchers like Mestas have been skittish about reopening the border, and not just because they worry screwworm could hitch a ride on Mexican cattle. US ranchers who don’t rely on Mexican cattle worry that bringing foreign livestock into the country could lower cattle prices, currently at historic highs. American consumers have been struggling with soaring beef prices for over two years now, but the elevated cost of livestock has been a relief for those ranchers, who feel they’re finally being paid fairly for their work. “These past few years, I actually made money!” Mestas said, with an audible hint of amazement. “Years and years, it was basically always break-even.” Beef prices, along with the broader cost of living, are also a salient political issue ahead of the 2026 midterms. Jenna Stanton, director of policy with the US Cattlemen’s Association (USCA), told CNN that many ranchers see the Trump administration’s push to open the border as an attempt to ease market pressures and lower the cost of beef. The White House had previously angered US ranchers by quadrupling low-tariff imports of Argentine beef to cool prices. On Friday, the president announced that the US would import 300,000 metric tons of beef to “reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.” The decision quickly drew criticism from cattle industry organizations. “There’s a midterm to be won this fall that, frankly, they are losing,” said Stanton. “They are looking to pull any lever they can.” CNN asked USDA about whether beef prices and the upcoming midterm elections had any bearing on the decision to reopen the Douglas port. The agency responded by sending CNN an op-ed by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins that mentioned neither the elections nor beef prices. “If at any point we determine there is an imminent threat to our domestic herd, we will not hesitate to immediately pause the reopenings,” Rollins wrote. “Protecting American livestock will always come first, and we will continue using every tool at our disposal to support the ranchers who raise them and to eliminate (screwworm) once and for all.” Cries for economic protectionism by some ranchers and crises of animal health like screwworm often go hand-in-hand, according to agricultural historian Bill Winders of Georgia Tech. Bullard’s organization R-CALF similarly argued for a border closure with Canada during an outbreak of mad cow disease, a fatal brain-destroying condition, among Canadian livestock in the early 2000s. That closure lasted over two years. “These kinds of moments are often seized upon by organizations interested in protectionism,” said Winders. “And it can often help their position, even if just in the short term.” Winders notes that R-CALF only represents one part of the larger cattle supply chain. Numerous other agricultural organizations are in favor of the phased reopening, such as the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), a trade association for ranchers and feeders, including many who rely on Mexican livestock. The NCBA didn’t respond to multiple CNN requests for comment, but said in a statement posted online that the border reopening will “help normalize business for cattle operations throughout the border states and Southern Plains.” A ‘destroyed’ market Derrell Peel, a professor of agricultural economics at Oklahoma State University, is skeptical of R-CALF’s narrative about the benefits of border closures for the US cattle industry. Peel, who is an expert on the Mexican cattle trade, told CNN that screwworm isn’t the primary force behind high cattle prices, and sees the issue as a fig-leaf for a broader anti-free trade agenda. The high prices are due to the US cattle herd – the total population of cattle and calves in the US – being at a 75 year low after years of frequent, severe droughts, he said. That lack of supply, not just the screwworm, has pushed prices up. “We would have had record cattle prices (in the US) with or without the border closed,” Peel said. In the meantime, Peel added, Mexican ranchers have lost up to a thousand dollars per animal since the border closed to the livestock trade. One of those ranchers is Bustillos, the union head in Chihuahua, who declined to put a dollar figure on the money he’s lost to the border closure. “I lost a bunch of money,” Bustillos said. Closing the border to the cattle trade “destroyed the dynamics of the market.” He also worries about his colleagues in the US meatpacking industry, many of whom relied on Mexican exports to make their bottom line. Cattle that might have come to the US and fattened on American corn to be turned into steaks are now fed, slaughtered and packed entirely in Mexico – then sent to the US as boxed beef. According to USDA data, Mexico has exported 22% more boxed beef to the US this year. US meatpackers are responding with cutbacks. Last week, major meatpacking company Tyson Foods announced it is closing plants in Illinois and Utah and seeking to sell a facility in Washington, citing “one of the most historic cattle shortages the country has ever experienced.” “These cattle (in Mexico) had to go somewhere,” Bustillos said, “What the US doesn’t understand is they’re going to give all that leverage to Mexico as an industry.” Mexico has built out its ability to export beef significantly over the years, said Peel. He warns that the border closure’s disruption could last a long time. “The fact that (Mexico is now) absorbing those exportable cattle that they have not been exporting will probably lead to changes in the supply chain,” said Peel, “It might become more permanent in nature.” As for the animal health risk, many proponents point out that screwworm made it into the US either through infested wildlife or via flies themselves while the border was closed to the cattle trade. Sam Garcia, a Mexican American rancher and scientist who raises cattle in Sonora, told CNN that any livestock entering the US will be inspected numerous times for screwworm before being dipped in a chemical bath. Bleeding ranchers While expensive cattle may have given some American cattle producers breathing room, ranchers who spoke with CNN emphasized that high prices haven’t ensured easy wealth. Ranching is still difficult and often unprofitable work, especially for family operations. “Can we stop the bleed of the American rancher?” asks Cooper Little, the director of the Independent Cattleman’s Association of Texas. It’s a question he says he often poses when speaking with the thousands of small cattle ranchers in his organization, many of whom are elderly and struggling to stay afloat despite better revenue from high prices. Little, who speaks with an unmistakable Texas twang, saw the border closure as a chance to reshore the US cattle industry and stop the bleed. Without competition from Mexican producers, people might “have an interest in entering the beef cattle industry and being the legacy of their father or grandfather.” “It’s a hard life,” Little says of ranching. “And it’s getting harder every year.” J Storme Birdwell, who runs her family’s ranch on the Texas Gulf Coast, says day-to-day cattle production is a struggle. As expensive as cattle are, land is worth more. In recent years, Birdwell says she’s had trouble retaining leased plots of pastureland as younger generations of ranching families choose to cash out and sell rather than stay in the harsh world of agriculture. Those struggles are also intimately familiar to Mexican ranchers. Garcia, the Mexican American who raises cattle in Sonora, emphasizes that US and Mexican cattle producers are more similar than they are different, despite competing interests. “I can tell you,” Garcia said. “I have more in common with an American rancher than a politician in New York.” “The difference is labor might be cheaper down in Mexico, but also there’s not that many government incentives to be more productive” compared to the US, he said. Another of those shared issues is the lack of water. Ten years ago, Johnny Mestas in Colorado says he nearly lost his herd due to an expensive fight over water rights. Drought is an insidious threat to ranching life, and it’s only getting worse with climate change. “Some of my neighbors think I’m one rich sucker,” Mestas said, “But they don’t know half the sh–t we went through.”

articles.summary: Pakistan News: The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for.
articles.body: The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for what it described as "sensitive security duties".The decision allows three companies of the Pakistan Army to be deployed in the city under Article 245 of the Pakistani Constitution, which permits the armed forces to assist the civil administration in maintaining security."The federal government, exercising the powers conferred under Article 245 of the Constitution of Pakistan, is pleased to authorise the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army for sensitive security duties in Rawalpindi," according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control on Friday.The notification said the deployment was intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities could respond quickly if an unexpected situation arose.It said that the decision was taken "to avoid any undesirable situation as well as to respond effectively in any unforeseen situation as per the requirement of the district administration".Army deployment follows security incidentThe decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party opened fire at security forces in Rawalpindi. He was subsequently killed in retaliatory firing.State-run PTV News, citing security sources, reported that the attacker was a resident of Khyber district and an "active PTI member". According to the report, a PTI flag, bullets and weapons were recovered from him.The PTI, however, rejected any connection with the incident. The party said it had nothing to do with terrorism and accused authorities of attempting to associate the party with the attack.Rawalpindi has strategic importanceThe deployment is particularly significant because Rawalpindi is home to the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters, the military's top command centre.The city is therefore an important military and administrative centre, and the decision to deploy army personnel there comes amid heightened security concerns following the recent shooting incident.The deployment has been authorised for six months, with the troops to perform duties requested by the district administration under the constitutional provision allowing the military to assist civilian authorities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
