articles.title: This El Niño could become 'the largest in living memory', forecasters warn. Americans could feel the effects into 2027.
articles.summary: El Niño's effect will be felt in 2027, making it 'very likely' to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record globally.
articles.body:
The El Niño developing over the Pacific Ocean could be "the largest in living memory," according to the Met Office , the U.K.'s national weather service.

The climate phenomenon, which the Met Office is calling "unprecedented," can boost global temperatures and increase the likelihood of extreme weather. Forecasters said it's likely to become the largest of its kind since the 19th century, adding that 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record globally.

El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. It occurs naturally every two to seven years and tends to last between nine and 12 months.

The Met Office's latest forecasts show a rise of more than 5.4°F (3°C) in equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperatures later this year. A typical El Niño brings warming of 1.8°F to 3.6°F (1°C to 2°C), with 3.6°F (2°C) considered a major event.

"I have never seen a forecast that looks like this," Adam Scaife, a professor at the Met Office, told ITN News . "The strength of El Niño in our forecasts is already at very high levels, even at this early stage.

"It peaks in November, December, and by that stage, it looks very much like it's going to be a record event, the biggest in recent history, the biggest in living memory, and perhaps even the biggest for over a century."

The forecast is consistent with warnings from U.S. forecasters that a historically significant El Niño may be looming. Berkeley Earth , a nonprofit climate research group, found in July that there is a 90% chance tropical Pacific temperatures will exceed all records over about 150 years of observations. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center told Yahoo News it has classified the 2026 El Niño as ranking "among the largest El Niño events."

The Climate Prediction Center puts the odds at 69% that the event exceeds every El Niño measured since 1950 during the October-through-December stretch, and above 90% that it reaches "very strong" strength this fall and winter. The agency gives it a 97% chance of lasting into early spring 2027.

NOAA's outlook for December through February already shows a clear pattern taking shape, with the impacts of El Niño expected to become more pronounced as winter progresses.

"For the U.S., the impacts of El Niño are most clearly evident from fall through spring," Michelle L'Heureux, a physical scientist at NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, told Yahoo News.

"Generally speaking, El Niño tends to increase the storm track over the southern tier of the United States, increasing the chances of above-average precipitation," she added. "At the same time, because the storm track is shifted southward over the U.S., regions across the northern U.S. tend to be drier. The northern U.S. has the highest chances for above-average temperatures, too."

As it strengthens, El Niño's effects are expected to become increasingly apparent around the world — including in the U.S. Forecasters have predicted that warm summer temperatures, including the hottest July on record , may persist for longer than usual .

Parts of the Northeast were still experiencing hot and humid conditions this week as severe weather swept through the region. On Thursday, storms tore through a beach on Long Island, stranded dozens of people in cars in New Jersey and knocked out power in parts of Delaware's capital, the Associated Press reported.

Mike Lichniak, chief meteorologist at Delaware-area TV station WBOC , warned earlier that morning that rising humidity would push temperatures into the 80s and 90s, with a heat index above 100°F in some areas. Severe thunderstorms and an isolated tornado followed that afternoon and evening.

In NOAA's Climate Prediction Center seasonal temperature outlook for fall 2026, released on Aug. 20, the agency favors above-normal temperatures across nearly the entire country from September through November. The Pacific Northwest, the northern Rockies and parts of coastal Alaska have the highest odds, at 50% to 70%, of a warmer-than-normal season.

Much of the rest of the U.S., including the South, Midwest, Northeast and Florida, also has elevated odds of above-normal temperatures, at 33% to 50%.

The lone exception is a pocket of the Ohio Valley, covering parts of Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky and Missouri, where forecasters see "equal chances" of above-, near- or below-normal temperatures. No part of the country is expected to see a cooler-than-average fall.

The Climate Prediction Center's December-through-February outlook puts the wettest odds over Southern California, the southern tier and much of the East Coast, with its strongest confidence in the Southeast. The drier signal is confined to the northern tier, where the agency also expects above-normal temperatures.

That leaves the northern U.S. warm and dry, which is not the combination that produces heavy snow. The southern storm track can bring it instead to places that rarely get much.

articles.title: Red Lobster brings back Endless Shrimp after promotion helped push chain toward bankruptcy
articles.summary: Red Lobster rebuilt its Endless Shrimp promotion with stronger financial discipline and limited-time pricing after the permanent offer fueled bankruptcy.
articles.body: Red Lobster is once again offering its Endless Shrimp promotion that contributed to millions of dollars in losses before the seafood chain filed for bankruptcy two years ago. The company told Fox News Digital it decided to bring back Endless Shrimp because the promotion still matters enormously to its customers, who "never stopped asking for it." "They continued telling us they missed it, showed up when we brought it back this spring and kept asking for more after that run ended," Red Lobster said. AMERICA'S CHEAPEST POPCORN SHRIMP BASKET AT A CHAIN RESTAURANT COSTS UNDER $9 "We weren’t going to walk away from something they love simply because the previous operating model did not work," the company added. "The better answer was to fix what didn’t work and bring it back in a way that is right for our guests, our restaurant teams and the company." According to Red Lobster, the spring run also proved the company could bring Endless Shrimp back in a way "that delights our guests and works for our restaurant teams and our business." Participating locations began offering the current Endless Shrimp deal for a limited time Aug. 17. "Guests can mix and match five flavors endlessly throughout the meal for as much shrimp as they like, any way they like it," Red Lobster announced in a press release. The lineup includes new garlic bread-crusted shrimp, shrimp linguini Alfredo, garlic shrimp scampi, Parrot Isle coconut shrimp and Walt’s Favorite Shrimp, hand-breaded, butterflied shrimp lightly fried and served with cocktail sauce. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Red Lobster closed dozens of locations nationwide in May 2024 before filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, Fox News previously reported. Many analysts and media reports have cited the company’s decision to make Endless Shrimp a permanent offering as one factor behind its financial troubles. Endless Shrimp returned to select Red Lobster locations in the spring of 2026, but the chain’s 37-year-old CEO, Damola Adamolekun, made it clear in a statement to affiliate FOX 13 Tampa Bay that the promotion would be available for a limited time only. "The previous model did not work, so we did not repeat it," Red Lobster told Fox News Digital. "We rebuilt Endless Shrimp around much stronger operational and financial discipline, including better forecasting, kitchen flow, menu structure and restaurant support.  "We also designed the current offer to work as a dine-in experience, with pricing that can vary by market. The new standard is simple: Endless Shrimp has to work for the guest, the restaurant team and the business." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The spring run of Endless Shrimp "met and exceeded our expectations in several important ways," Red Lobster told Fox News Digital. "Guest satisfaction significantly outperformed the average for Red Lobster promotions, restaurant-team support was stronger than it had been in years and our internal team Proud to Serve and Recommend scores both came in above historical levels," the company said.  "Just as importantly, guests continued asking for Endless Shrimp after the promotion ended." In June 2026, Adamolekun said he was planning "the greatest comeback in the history of the restaurant industry." His plan includes streamlining operations, closing underperforming restaurants, increasing engagement with customers and tapping into their nostalgia. One of the biggest lessons Red Lobster said it learned from the previous Endless Shrimp promotion was that "guest demand alone is not enough." articles.title: Erin Patterson: The hotel booking snafu that could free mushroom murderer
articles.summary: A table tennis tournament and a throat lozenge could help Erin Patterson's lawyers overturn her convictions.
articles.body:
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.

But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.

This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.

The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.

But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.

"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.

When Patterson served her estranged husband's relatives a poisonous mushroom-laced lunch in 2023, killing three and gravely injuring another, she thrust the sleepy Gippsland region into the global spotlight.

The community of Korumburra, where the victims were beloved figures, became shrouded in grief. Leongatha, where Patterson lived, was gripped by shock. And Morwell, host of the lengthy trial, was overwhelmed by journalists, lawyers and spectators - as were towns nearby.

You couldn't walk down the main street without spotting some of the courtroom's stars, or grab a coffee without overhearing chatter about the case.

Mushroom murders and cancer lie: Nine weeks of evidence that gripped a courtroom

'Everyone knows somebody affected': The small towns in shock after mushroom murders

It was this frenzy from which the jury of 12 needed protection, the trial judge decided.

Jurors are required to consider only the evidence presented to them in court, and must only talk about the case among themselves. In Australia, these rules are so strict that discussion with outsiders is forbidden even after a trial wraps up.

To reduce the risk of contamination and the temptation of gossip, Justice Christopher Beale decided the jury should be sequestered once deliberations began - a relatively rare move which meant they would stay in supervised accommodation with little to no contact with the outside world until they reached a decision.

But finding the jury, and the jury keepers watching them, somewhere to sleep became something of a logistical nightmare.

As the trial dragged on, stays became longer than anyone anticipated and accommodation became a constant scramble.

And the week the table tennis tournament came to town - which by a stroke of bad luck was the one in which the jury finally retired - turned the accommodation drought into a famine.

At 08:28 on Monday 7 July, an email from the judge's chambers popped into the inboxes of the lawyers in the case.

It revealed that the lead detective who investigated the murders - a key trial witness - and two prosecution solicitors had been staying at the same hotel as the sequestered jury.

The jurors had exclusive use of a separate floor of the hotel, the email said, and had eaten their meals in a conference room, away from all other guests.

Common areas like the lobby were used by everyone, but the jury keeper who reported the issue said there had been no interaction between his charges and anyone from the prosecution case.

"I understand that there is a shortage of accommodation in the district, but it is obviously undesirable," Justice Beale wrote.

About two hours later, the prosecution responded, admitting they had been aware of the situation for days.

The detective "took steps to avoid common areas from the point that he became aware that [the jurors] were there", their email read.

Upon learning their team would cross over with the jury for a single night, the prosecution had done its best to find other hotels for staff. But they couldn't get alternative rooms for two solicitors, though the email stressed the pair also took steps to avoid any "incidental contact".

However, another missive from the judge's chambers quickly overshadowed the hotel mix-up that same afternoon: the jury had reached their verdicts.

They had found Patterson guilty on all counts.

Patterson's lawyers are now arguing the hotel mix-up amounted to a "fundamental irregularity" which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts.

"We would describe... it as catastrophic," Patterson's appeal counsel, Edney, told Victoria's Court of Appeal this week.

"What occurred here was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure in the process."

The defence - which Edney pointed out had been kept in the dark several days longer than anyone else - didn't immediately move for a mistrial last July.

Instead, it twice asked the state's juries commissioner to investigate in the weeks following the verdicts. Both requests were rejected, the barrister said, and the reasons have not been made public.

A year on, there remains a "vacuum of evidence" around what occurred during "the most critical week" of the entire trial, Edney argued.

There is no CCTV from the hotel; no sworn statements from those who were sharing it with the jury - a group which also includes an unknown number of journalists; and nothing to say what happened except the two brief emails sent last July.

There was also at least one media report at the time - raised by Edney this week but rubbished by the prosecution lawyers as "unverified" and "seemingly inaccurate" - that the mix-up had led to "people hiding in doorways to avoid contact" and "skipping breakfast".

"My question is... so what?" Justice Peter Kidd bit back.

In any criminal trial, jurors see other parties all the time - in corridors, or even nearby cafes - but they're under the constant supervision of jury keepers who have sworn to ensure there's no improper communication, he said.

Edney conceded there was "no evidence" that the jurors had communicated with anyone else, but said innocent contact - even just seeing the detective or solicitors - could have resulted in "subconscious influence".

"This was a hotel with windows," Edney said several times - a likely thing for it to have, someone from the judge's bench countered.

Patterson's team cited two cases to support their argument: one in which jurors were discharged when one was offered a throat lozenge by a defendant's relative during a coughing fit, and another in which a retrial was ordered after jurors caught a taxi without being escorted by a jury keeper.

"The system worked as it was intended to work," Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane KC said.

The jury was constantly supervised, and when a potential problem was identified, steps were immediately taken to prevent it becoming an actual issue.

The jury keeper, the lead detective, and the prosecution all say there was no contact.

"The evidence in this case is that there was no interaction between any other person and the jury," he said.

Other cases the defence pointed to in which jury errors resulted in retrials all had evidence of actual contact, he noted.

Patterson has seven appeal grounds - the others relating to rulings on evidence and alleged unfairness by the prosecution - but this one, by the defence's own admission, is unprecedented.

Just as important as actual interference is the perception of interference, said Edney, quoting the trial judge's own speech as he selected jury members on the very first day of the trial.

"Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done."

The trio of judges are now deliberating on Patterson's appeal, as well as an argument by the prosecution that her parole period should be scrapped.

They will announce their decisions at a later date.

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill two and injure others as Gaza attacks continue
articles.summary: Israeli drone attack targeted a family in the central city of Deir el-Balah, killing one person and wounding others.
articles.body:
At least two Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks in the last 48 hours, Gaza’s Ministry of Health says, as many victims of past strikes remain trapped under rubble, inaccessible to ambulance and rescue crews.

Four injured people were also brought to hospitals in Gaza, the Health Ministry said on Saturday.

list 1 of 3 Hundreds of children take part in swimming class on Gaza’s shore

list 2 of 3 Gaza is running out of places to bury the dead

list 3 of 3 Over 100 ex-diplomats urge France, UK to sanction Israel over Palestine

An Israeli drone attack targeted the al-Hasanat family in the central city of Deir el-Balah on Saturday, killing one person and wounding others, Al Jazeera’s Ashraf Abu Amra reported from the city.

Abu Amra said the attack was carried out without warning to the family, in an area crowded with tents of displaced people . Ambulance and civil defence crews rushed to the scene and transported several wounded people to Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in the city.

Abu Amra reported that the Israeli army carried out two demolition operations in Deir el-Balah, with explosions heard from a distance as the targeted houses collapsed into rubble.

Israeli forces also pushed into the eastern part of the city and struck multiple homes there, he said, with troops remaining positioned close to civilian areas along the city’s eastern perimeter.

Israeli strikes and home demolitions continued elsewhere in the enclave, including in the southern city of Khan Younis. In eastern Khan Younis, Israeli forces shelled several civilian areas, targeting displaced Palestinians’ camps sitting across from the military-controlled area along the “Yellow Line” .

Israeli forces have advanced further into the east of Gaza City, expanding the “Yellow Line” towards more civilian areas and demolishing property and infrastructure inside the zone.

According to local reports, a woman was wounded after being fired at by Israeli forces near ad-Dawa Street, northeast of the Nuseirat refugee camp, in an attack on civilians in central Gaza.

There were also Israeli artillery attacks in areas northeast of the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza, as they continued firing in the eastern parts of the Strip.

Abu Amra said Israeli air and artillery attacks have intensified in areas the military designates as “ humanitarian zones ”, where more than two million people are concentrated in roughly 30 percent of the Gaza Strip’s total area.

Despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed to in October 2025, Gaza’s Health Ministry said on Saturday that 1,285 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. Overall, since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023, 73,419 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, most of them women and children.

The toll remains incomplete, authorities say, as thousands are feared trapped under the rubble of destroyed buildings. As families retrieve bodies of their loved ones, Gaza is also running out of space to bury the dead.

images.caption: Palestinian mourners carry flag-draped body bags containing the remains of Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks that were recently recovered from the rubble, during a mass funeral in Gaza City on August 20, 2026 [Omar al-Qattaa/AFP]

articles.title: Israeli army and settlers injure several Palestinians across West Bank
articles.summary: Palestinians face attacks and forced displacement as settlers expand control, backed by military raids and inaction.
articles.body:
Israeli military raids and attacks by Israelis from illegal settlements across the occupied West Bank have injured at least 19 Palestinians, according to Palestinian health officials and local media reports.

Israeli forces shot and injured three Palestinians who attempted to enter occupied East Jerusalem near the separation wall in ar-Ram, the Jerusalem Governorate said on Saturday.

list 2 of 3 Palestinian teen shot and killed in West Bank attack, UN responds

list 3 of 3 Palestinian victims of Israeli settler attacks face battle for justice

It said the incident was part of near-daily attacks against Palestinian workers barred from their jobs in Israel since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

In the Tubas Governorate in northern West Bank, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said its crews treated at least 11 Palestinians, including four children, for tear gas inhalation during Israeli army raids.

In Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, an elderly man was beaten and bruised by armed settlers, after which Israeli forces raided his home, damaged its contents and confiscated his family’s phones, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

The Palestine Red Crescent also reported that two young men were hospitalised after being beaten by Israeli settlers in Arrabeh, south of Jenin, while a 15-year-old boy was hospitalised after a severe beating by settlers in Tammun, in Tubas province, where another child was injured in a settler assault.

In separate attacks on Friday, the Israeli army and settlers killed two Palestinians in Hebron and in Jenin.

Meanwhile in Qusra , south of Nablus, the Hassan and Abu Rida families remain besieged in their homes for a 14th consecutive day by settlers, with Israeli forces maintaining a closed military zone around the site.

Residents accuse the army of inaction, which amounts to complicity in the families’ possible forced displacement.

The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said Israeli settlers now number roughly 780,000 across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, living among 192 settlements and 400 outposts, rising to 71 percent of Area C and 91 percent of the Jordan Valley, the commission said.

The United Nations humanitarian affairs office recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank between January and late July, averaging roughly six a day and marking the fastest pace since the agency began systematic tracking two decades ago.

More than 2,300 Palestinians have been forced from their homes so far this year due to settler violence or the restrictions that accompany it, according to UN figures. Separately, a UN-appointed commission of inquiry has found that Israeli authorities repeatedly failed to prevent foreseeable settler attacks and, in some cases, directly enabled them through army protection and the provision of weapons and funding.

articles.title: Lucy Davis 'grateful' for support after cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The Office star was appearing at convention in London, less than two weeks after announcing her condition.
articles.body:
Actress Lucy Davis has told fans she is "grateful" for their support as she made an appearance at a London sci-fi convention, following the recent revelation she has incurable breast cancer.

The 53-year-old star was appearing at the For The Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention at Excel London on Saturday, less than two weeks after announcing her diagnosis in a post on Instagram.

Davis, who was on a panel to talk about her role in the 2004 zombie-comedy Shaun of the Dead, told an audience of hundreds of people about the interactions she had enjoyed with the film's fans during the event.

"It's like this whole second family you never knew you had, everyone is like a community, friendly, supportive of not only us but you guys and each other," she said. "We need a bit more niceness in the world, so I'm grateful."

Lucy Davis urges women to check their breasts for cancer - here's how

The Office actress Lucy Davis says she has 'incurable' cancer

It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.

She said in that announcement it had "metastasised" to her bones following a diagnosis a year-and-half-ago, meaning it was "too late" for chemotherapy.

Davis signed autographs and posed for photographs before appearing on Saturday's panel.

Some fans posing questions told the actress "I love you so much", but she was not asked directly about her health.

The Shaun of the Dead director, Edgar Wright, and Simon Pegg, who played the lead role in the cult British movie, were also on the panel. Davis portrayed Dianne, an aspiring actress who was one of the core group of survivors of a zombie apocalypse, and helps Pegg's character Shaun fight off the legions of the undead.

Her favourite memories of filming, she said, were "when we all pretended to be zombies and walked across the square; it was like being naughty schoolkids.

The actress, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom The Office and whose father is comedian Jasper Carrott, was also applauded when asked for advice about getting into the film industry.

She said: "We all grow up with a different life with a different world telling us we all have limitations.

"None of us do, our only limitations are things that we think are limiting. We can do anything, or be anybody, and don't apologise for that."

Davis had thanked fans for their "kindness and support" in another post two days after revealing she had cancer.

"OK, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," she said.

"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."

articles.title: Tropical Storm Moke advances towards Hawaii with heavy rain, strong winds
articles.summary: For the second week in a row, Hawaii Island, also known as the Big Island, faces threats from an intensifying storm.
articles.body:
Tropical Storm Moke is grinding towards Hawaii, bringing gusts of wind and heavy rain only a week after the islands faced similar conditions from Hurricane Lala.

On Saturday, Hawaii residents prepared for the latest storm, which is expected to pass south of Hawaii Island, the largest island in the Hawaiian archipelago, overnight and into the following morning.

list 1 of 3 Hurricane Lala weakens to a tropical storm, but flooding persists in Hawaii

list 2 of 3 Storm Lala strengthens into a Category 1 hurricane as it nears Hawaii

list 3 of 3 Tropical Storm Lala leaves Hawaii flooded and without power

As of 11am Hawaii Standard Time (21:00 GMT), Moke was located about 684 kilometres, or 425 miles, south of Hilo, a city on the eastern coast of Hawaii Island. It was moving west-northwest at 19km/h (12mph).

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) in the United States reported that the storm’s maximum sustained winds were about 85km/h (50mph).

Moke, like Lala, is forecast to spare the Big Island a potentially disastrous direct hit. But the island is still recovering from Lala, a Category 1 storm that spurred heavy flooding and power outages.

At least one person died in last weekend’s storm.

Lala came close enough to Hawaii Island to dump more than 1,000mm (39 inches) of rain in some locations, causing rivers to burst their banks.

High winds also bent tall palm trees and downed electrical lines, forcing nearly 130,000 utility customers to lose power.

Hawaii Governor Josh Green and other state officials have urged people to prepare for Moke by restocking food, medicine and other daily essentials ahead of the storm’s passage.

“It could certainly have a big impact because we’ve already been hit hard,” Green said in a video statement. “We’re pre-positioning all kinds of additional equipment and people. I’ve also authorised 100 rooms, hotel rooms, for people to go to, in case they don’t have enough services or protection, safety.”

Green added that, while power had been restored to most of Hawaii Island after Lala, some remote areas were still experiencing outages. Power is expected to be fully restored by September 8.

After passing Hawaii Island during the night, Moke is projected to continue on a westward path near the islands through early Tuesday, according to Casey Oswant, a meteorologist with the Honolulu office of the US National Weather Service.

“There will still be impacts, especially to the windward and southeast sides of the Big Island, but it will probably be a little bit more limited than what we saw with Lala,” Oswant said.

The National Hurricane Center projects that Moke will bring roughly 130mm to 250mm (5 to 10 inches) of rainfall over the next two days on the southeast and windward sides of the Big Island. Some isolated areas could see as much as 380mm (15 inches).

Eastern Maui, meanwhile, is likely to receive 76mm to 150mm (3 to 6 inches), with smaller amounts of precipitation expected across the rest of the island chain.

Governor Green warned that the heavy rain is unlikely to end with Moke.

“Everyone be very careful,” he said. “This storm will be followed by another storm front about a week later, and we continue to see the impacts of these major weather fronts that have hit Hawaii.”

articles.title: Energy UK says struggling households need more support with bills
articles.summary: Industry body Energy UK says the current support for households most in need does not go far enough.
articles.body:
Higher energy bills this winter mean the government should step in to provide more help for households most in need, the body representing energy firms in the UK has said.

Stubbornly high prices over the last few years have left some people needing "emergency support" over and above the existing £150 Warm Home Discount, Energy UK said.

A "better targeted" support scheme that takes into account someone's income, health and energy consumption was needed, it added.

On Wednesday, the energy price cap for October onwards will be announced by regulator Ofgem and is expected to hit a three-year high.

A government spokesperson said that in addition to the Warm Homes Discount it was cutting VAT on electricity bills and would do "everything we can" to shield consumers from global energy shocks.

Energy UK chief executive Dhara Vyas said: "Suppliers continue to do all they can to help their customers but as well as persistently high bills, record levels of debt show how the current system is failing to provide the right support to those in need."

A new "social discount" scheme would result in "a system that works better for everyone", she added.

Energy UK says suppliers have a range of support measures for customers that includes debt write-off schemes and hardship funds, as well as enhanced funding to charity partners.

However, Adam Scorer, chief executive at National Energy Action (NEA) said: "Heading toward winter with prices spiking again we expect suppliers to do more - listen and respond to their customer who are really struggling.

"More than anything else people need a responsible and empathetic approach to debt," he added.

Ofgem reported at the end of last winter that customers who had fallen behind on their energy bills owed suppliers a record £4.7bn. Since then wholesale energy prices have risen, following the start of the Iran war in February.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight predicts Ofgem's cap on household price rises, which is set every three months, will go up by 4% when it is announced on Wednesday.

The rise will apply to household bills during the first half of the coming winter and follows a sharper 13% rise in July.

The energy cap covers around 33 million households in England, Wales and Scotland.

It fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used, but households' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it.

As well as the conflict in the Middle East, Cornwall Insight said prices had been affected by heatwaves across Europe that had increased demand for power generation to support air conditioning and other cooling.

The price rise would outweigh the impact of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's move to remove VAT on household electricity bills from October, it added.

Currently, people receiving means-tested benefits are entitled to the one-off £150 Warm Home Discount over the winter, something administered by the energy suppliers themselves. The rebate is paid for by a levy on all energy users that is collected and redistributed via bills.

Energy UK said the Warm Home Discount reached six million customers, but there were another 2.5 million who needed help because a medical condition or draughty home meant they consumed more energy.

It said if the government would allow the combining of information about customers' income, health and energy consumption, a discount scheme could offer targeted and adjustable support, and respond to changing needs and price levels.

The body said its proposed new scheme would cost £1.9bn - nearly double the cost of the current scheme - but could offer £450 in support to some households.

Energy UK suggested the new support scheme could continue to be part-funded through bills or shifted entirely onto the taxpayer, via government funding.

The last time the price cap reached a similar level was in July 2023, Cornwall Insight said, which was still below the peaks reached the previous year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

During that energy price spike the Conservative government committed a total of around £40bn of government spending to support households with energy bills.

The challenge of combining sources of personal data, including income and health, and the proposal to find more taxpayer money to fund such a scheme are likely to raise questions.

However, Adam Scorer from the NEA said this was the sort of approach his charity was calling for, especially as the Warm Home Discount has risen by only £10 over the last decade.

"We desperately need a new approach," he said.

"There will be a lot of detail to get right, but if government genuinely wants to provide breathing space for people in fuel poverty, it needs to take this challenge on and work with energy companies and charities to design something truly fit for purpose."

articles.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
articles.summary: Teachers warn it could be increasingly difficult for classrooms to function during the hottest months.
articles.body:
Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.

It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and Aâlevel students sitting exams during extreme heat.

Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an examâ¦ so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

So, is it going to be increasingly difficult for schools to operate in the summer months? And is moving the school summer holidays the solution to ensuring pupils are able to be taught for as much of the year as possible?

This summer is likely to become the hottest on record, according to the Met Office. Multiple temperature records have been broken with five widespread heatwaves and four consecutive months where the temperature has exceeded 35C. This has never happened before.

June saw one of the UK's most intense heatwaves, with up to seven consecutive days where temperatures were well above the official heatwave thresholds of 25-28C - just as the exam period was in full swing. Temperature records were broken too: 38C was recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June, the hottest June day ever measured in the UK.

The Met Office issued a red extreme heat warning at the end of June, while the UK Health Security Agency has issued multiple amber warnings over the last few months. The heat then continued into July, with heatwave conditions felt widely for most of the month.

Schools struggled to cope, with some closed declaring "heat days" as temperatures in classrooms became too high for children to concentrate. These kinds of disruptions, or heat days, could become more likely as human-induced climate change brings hotter summers and more frequent heatwaves.

Summer heat is arriving earlier. Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office, says the "de facto 'hot season' in the UK is lengthening, with increasing prevalence of hot weather - including heatwaves â in May and September in addition to the standard meteorological summer of June, July and August".

It's one sign of a warming climate reshaping the pattern and timing of UK summers.

According to a study conducted by the Met Office and University College London, students could lose an estimated 8.2 days of learning a year on average due to extreme heat, if average global average temperatures rise to more than 2C above pre-industiral levels - as many scientists believe will happen on current trajectories.

In the meantime, teachers are left to deal with the consequences.

Steve Chalke, founder of Oasis Academy, which runs more than 50 schools across England, says the heatwaves were a "real inhibitor" to teaching. One of the most difficult challenges came when the Met Office issued the red extreme heat warning at the end of June, suggesting potential "danger to life".

He says headteachers were forced into difficult decisions. "What do you do as a headteacher? How can they run a school safely if the national weather service is warning to travel only if essential and make every effort to stay cool. What if a student or member of staff collapses due to the heat and you're accountable for why you opened the school and didn't take your duty of care seriously?"

And with Met Office predictions of more extreme weather, higher summer temperatures, and more frequent, prolonged heatwaves, these types of questions are likely to only become more prevalent.

Rebecca Martin is concerned about her son taking GCSE exams in a few years' time in potentially increasingly hot weather. She thinks there needs to be "some serious considerations to the school year to reflect the changing climate or better investment in schools to give them air conditioning".

And there is growing evidence to support her worries. The recent Well-Adapted UK report from the Climate Change Committee suggested that taking an exam on a 32C day leads to around a 10% lower likelihood of passing, compared to sitting the same exam at 22C.

Baroness Brown told the BBC that "as heatwaves become more frequent and intense, it is unacceptable that children are expected to sit high-stakes exams in halls that were not designed for these conditions".

Many of us are familiar with a "snow day" in the winter, when snow can make it very difficult for staff and students to get into school. While there is no legal minimum temperature, the National Education Union says classrooms should be kept above 18C. Heat days are a newer concept - and there are no specified maximum temperatures for a classroom.

A 2024 study published in the journal Climate Risk Management suggested that any temperature above 24C can compromise learning. It also found a decline in student performance ranging from 2% to 12% for each degree increase in classroom temperature.

Setting a temperature benchmark of 26C as the upper "comfortable limit" in a classroom, the authors of the study went on to suggest that the average school currently reaches this limit 59 days of the year in England. That would increase to 71 days with 2C of warming.

In "at-risk" schools where there is no suitable ventilation or where newer buildings have lower ceilings, there would be 75 days where the "comfortable 26C classroom temperature would be breached".

In hotter European countries such as France and Spain, local authorities have extreme heat guidelines that trigger timetable changes or school closures when conditions become too hot. It's a model some argue the UK may need to consider as the UK summer continues to change.

While extreme heat or heatwaves can still occur in May and June - or indeed in late August or early September, by which time it's proposed pupils would have returned to class - breaking up for summer at the end of June could reduce the amount of disruption schools face from the hottest conditions heading into the peak of summer.

And while this August has also been hot and dry, some parents argue that an earlier break would be better aligned with the UK's typically warmer and drier mid-summer weather. Rebecca Martin says she'd like to be able to "make the most of the more guaranteed summer-like weather in July" planning to spend more time outdoors in a UK staycation rather than going abroad to parts of Europe where the "heat is getting even more extreme and unpleasant".

Europe is the fastest-warming continent, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average. Like the UK, European heatwaves are becoming hotter, more frequent and longer.

Staycations in the UK could become even more popular. According to 2024 research by Mintel, more than half of UK holidaymakers say they are likely to choose to holiday at home rather than abroad for climate-related reasons. Meanwhile, some 28% say higher UK temperatures are encouraging them to take domestic holidays.

What remains to be seen is how any changes to the school summer holiday could affect the price tag. Aligning the holiday period more closely with Scotland and other countries means there could be more demand in late June and July, potentially pushing the traditional price peak earlier in the year.

Other changing holiday habits - such as avoiding the peak of the summer heat and extreme temperatures in southern Europe - will also play a role.

In a recent national survey by InsureandGo, more than seven in 10 UK holidaymakers thought some European countries like Spain, Greece or Turkey would be too hot to visit in the summer months by the end of the decade.

As travel journalist Simon Calder has said: "A significant shift in holiday habits could push up the cost of a domestic holiday.

"If more people decide to stay in the UK, and others come to Britain because it is more climatically appealing, the rise in demand would trigger price increases. But there are always locations where you can get reasonable deals."

articles.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
articles.summary: Teachers warn it could be increasingly difficult for classrooms to function during the hottest months.
articles.body:
Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.

It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and A‑level students sitting exams during extreme heat.

Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an exam… so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

So, is it going to be increasingly difficult for schools to operate in the summer months? And is moving the school summer holidays the solution to ensuring pupils are able to be taught for as much of the year as possible?

This summer is likely to become the hottest on record, according to the Met Office. Multiple temperature records have been broken with five widespread heatwaves and four consecutive months where the temperature has exceeded 35C. This has never happened before.

June saw one of the UK's most intense heatwaves, with up to seven consecutive days where temperatures were well above the official heatwave thresholds of 25-28C - just as the exam period was in full swing. Temperature records were broken too: 38C was recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June, the hottest June day ever measured in the UK.

The Met Office issued a red extreme heat warning at the end of June, while the UK Health Security Agency has issued multiple amber warnings over the last few months. The heat then continued into July, with heatwave conditions felt widely for most of the month.

Schools struggled to cope, with some closed declaring "heat days" as temperatures in classrooms became too high for children to concentrate. These kinds of disruptions, or heat days, could become more likely as human-induced climate change brings hotter summers and more frequent heatwaves.

Summer heat is arriving earlier. Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office, says the "de facto 'hot season' in the UK is lengthening, with increasing prevalence of hot weather - including heatwaves – in May and September in addition to the standard meteorological summer of June, July and August".

It's one sign of a warming climate reshaping the pattern and timing of UK summers.

According to a study conducted by the Met Office and University College London, students could lose an estimated 8.2 days of learning a year on average due to extreme heat, if average global average temperatures rise to more than 2C above pre-industiral levels - as many scientists believe will happen on current trajectories.

In the meantime, teachers are left to deal with the consequences.

Steve Chalke, founder of Oasis Academy, which runs more than 50 schools across England, says the heatwaves were a "real inhibitor" to teaching. One of the most difficult challenges came when the Met Office issued the red extreme heat warning at the end of June, suggesting potential "danger to life".

He says headteachers were forced into difficult decisions. "What do you do as a headteacher? How can they run a school safely if the national weather service is warning to travel only if essential and make every effort to stay cool. What if a student or member of staff collapses due to the heat and you're accountable for why you opened the school and didn't take your duty of care seriously?"

And with Met Office predictions of more extreme weather, higher summer temperatures, and more frequent, prolonged heatwaves, these types of questions are likely to only become more prevalent.

Rebecca Martin is concerned about her son taking GCSE exams in a few years' time in potentially increasingly hot weather. She thinks there needs to be "some serious considerations to the school year to reflect the changing climate or better investment in schools to give them air conditioning".

And there is growing evidence to support her worries. The recent Well-Adapted UK report from the Climate Change Committee suggested that taking an exam on a 32C day leads to around a 10% lower likelihood of passing, compared to sitting the same exam at 22C.

Baroness Brown told the BBC that "as heatwaves become more frequent and intense, it is unacceptable that children are expected to sit high-stakes exams in halls that were not designed for these conditions".

Many of us are familiar with a "snow day" in the winter, when snow can make it very difficult for staff and students to get into school. While there is no legal minimum temperature, the National Education Union says classrooms should be kept above 18C. Heat days are a newer concept - and there are no specified maximum temperatures for a classroom.

A 2024 study published in the journal Climate Risk Management suggested that any temperature above 24C can compromise learning. It also found a decline in student performance ranging from 2% to 12% for each degree increase in classroom temperature.

Setting a temperature benchmark of 26C as the upper "comfortable limit" in a classroom, the authors of the study went on to suggest that the average school currently reaches this limit 59 days of the year in England. That would increase to 71 days with 2C of warming.

In "at-risk" schools where there is no suitable ventilation or where newer buildings have lower ceilings, there would be 75 days where the "comfortable 26C classroom temperature would be breached".

In hotter European countries such as France and Spain, local authorities have extreme heat guidelines that trigger timetable changes or school closures when conditions become too hot. It's a model some argue the UK may need to consider as the UK summer continues to change.

While extreme heat or heatwaves can still occur in May and June - or indeed in late August or early September, by which time it's proposed pupils would have returned to class - breaking up for summer at the end of June could reduce the amount of disruption schools face from the hottest conditions heading into the peak of summer.

And while this August has also been hot and dry, some parents argue that an earlier break would be better aligned with the UK's typically warmer and drier mid-summer weather. Rebecca Martin says she'd like to be able to "make the most of the more guaranteed summer-like weather in July" planning to spend more time outdoors in a UK staycation rather than going abroad to parts of Europe where the "heat is getting even more extreme and unpleasant".

Europe is the fastest-warming continent, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average. Like the UK, European heatwaves are becoming hotter, more frequent and longer.

Staycations in the UK could become even more popular. According to 2024 research by Mintel, more than half of UK holidaymakers say they are likely to choose to holiday at home rather than abroad for climate-related reasons. Meanwhile, some 28% say higher UK temperatures are encouraging them to take domestic holidays.

What remains to be seen is how any changes to the school summer holiday could affect the price tag. Aligning the holiday period more closely with Scotland and other countries means there could be more demand in late June and July, potentially pushing the traditional price peak earlier in the year.

Other changing holiday habits - such as avoiding the peak of the summer heat and extreme temperatures in southern Europe - will also play a role.

In a recent national survey by InsureandGo, more than seven in 10 UK holidaymakers thought some European countries like Spain, Greece or Turkey would be too hot to visit in the summer months by the end of the decade.

As travel journalist Simon Calder has said: "A significant shift in holiday habits could push up the cost of a domestic holiday.

articles.title: Kenya's gold rush: Was it sparked by the discovery of a $200 nugget by a goat herder?
articles.summary: Prospectors have come to West Pokot county in the hope a gram of the precious metal can change their lives.
articles.body:
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.

When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor.

And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.

It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.

Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.

People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.

Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.

"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.

Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.

"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.

Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.

Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.

Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.

Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.

Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.

Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.

"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.

Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.

But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.

Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.

Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.

While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.

"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.

Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).

West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.

Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.

He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.

However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.

"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.

So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.

"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.

For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.

More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.

Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.

"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.

But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.

"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."

For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."

Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.

Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.

The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.

Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.

Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.

Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.

Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.

Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.

For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.

He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.

"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.

He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.

"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

articles.title: Incêndio deixa 6 feridos e ameaça 90 mil pessoas nos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Fogo avançou rapidamente em Reno, destruiu casas e obrigou 42 mil pessoas a deixarem suas residências; outras 45 mil estão sob alerta de evacuação.
articles.summary: Fogo avançou rapidamente em Reno, destruiu casas e obrigou 42 mil pessoas a deixarem suas residências; outras 45 mil estão sob alerta de evacuação.
articles.body:
Um incêndio de grandes proporções destruiu casas e avançou rapidamente pelo noroeste de Reno, no estado de Nevada , nos Estados Unidos , neste domingo (23). Segundo as autoridades, o fogo foi provocado por ação humana e ainda não havia sido controlado até a última atualização desta reportagem .

Ao menos seis pessoas ficaram feridas, sendo três moradores e três integrantes das equipes de emergência.

Serviço Postal dos EUA divulga norma de 95 páginas para restringir voto por correio

Canadá anuncia tarifas de retaliação às novas taxas dos EUA a partir de 8 de setembro

Juíza anula suspensão de vistos imposta por governo Trump a 75 países

O incêndio, chamado de Hawk Fire, começou no sábado (22) e rapidamente se espalhou por uma área de cerca de 53 km². As chamas avançaram pela região de Peavine Peak, na Floresta Nacional Humboldt-Toiyabe, próxima à fronteira com a Califórnia.

O fogo se espalhou com velocidade durante a noite de sábado. Segundo o xerife do condado de Washoe, Darin Balaam, as chamas chegaram a passar por cima de caminhões dos bombeiros, dificultando o trabalho das equipes enquanto moradores tentavam deixar a região.

“Foi extremamente confuso”, disse Balaam. Segundo ele, a mudança na direção dos ventos fez com que as chamas avançassem para diferentes áreas.

Várias estruturas foram destruídas. As autoridades não informaram como o incêndio começou e disseram que o caso está sendo investigado.

Cerca de 90 mil pessoas são orientadas a deixar a região

Cerca de 42 mil moradores receberam uma ordem de evacuação imediata depois que a área classificada como “SAIA AGORA” foi ampliada até os arredores da Universidade de Nevada.

Outras 45 mil pessoas estão em uma área de alerta para possível evacuação. As autoridades pediram que todos deixem a região e estejam preparados para permanecer longe de casa por vários dias.

A previsão era de que os ventos ficassem mais fortes e mudassem de direção, o que poderia tornar o avanço das chamas ainda mais imprevisível.

“Por favor, saiam agora, se puderem”, disse o xerife.

O governador de Nevada, Joe Lombardo, decretou estado de emergência no condado de Washoe. A Guarda Nacional de Nevada foi mobilizada para ajudar no combate aéreo e na segurança das áreas evacuadas.

Ao todo, cerca de 800 profissionais atuavam no combate ao incêndio.

Quase 10 mil clientes estavam sem energia elétrica no condado de Washoe neste domingo. No sábado, o número chegou a 60 mil.

Trechos da rodovia U.S. 395, uma das principais ligações entre o norte e o sul da região, também foram fechados.

Reno tem mais de 280 mil habitantes e é a maior cidade de Nevada fora da região metropolitana de Las Vegas.

As autoridades abriram o Centro de Convenções Reno-Sparks para receber os moradores retirados de suas casas. Animais, porém, não foram permitidos no local. Pequenos e grandes animais foram encaminhados para dois outros pontos.

Cassinos de Reno ofereceram descontos em quartos de hotel para pessoas afetadas pelas evacuações.

Família tentou salvar pertences antes de perder a casa

Cari Kieffer descobriu neste domingo que sua casa havia sido completamente destruída pelo incêndio. Segundo ela, apenas uma cesta de basquete permaneceu de pé.

“Eu acordei esta manhã e comecei a chorar. Meus filhos perderam tudo”, disse Kieffer. “Tudo o que temos desapareceu.”

No sábado, ela assistia ao jogo de futebol americano do filho quando soube que a casa da família, nos arredores de Reno, estava em uma área de evacuação.

Segundo Kieffer, o aplicativo usado pela família para acompanhar o avanço do incêndio mostrava uma localização muito atrasada em relação às chamas. Por isso, eles acreditaram que os bombeiros haviam conseguido impedir que o fogo chegasse ao bairro.

Quando perceberam o risco, Kieffer, o marido e os quatro filhos, com idades entre 3 e 16 anos, correram para retirar os cachorros e alguns objetos da casa.

Cinzas caíam sobre a região enquanto o vento levava o calor das chamas em direção ao bairro.

“As chamas ficavam cada vez mais perto toda vez que eu olhava para fora”, contou Kieffer. “Eu pensei: temos que ir agora.”

Com os olhos lacrimejando e a garganta ardendo por causa da fumaça, ela conseguiu pegar algumas roupas, uma Bíblia, fotos do casamento e as cinzas da mãe.

Na correria, enquanto bombeiros gritavam para que a família deixasse o local imediatamente, ela esqueceu documentos importantes, como as certidões de nascimento dos filhos. Também não conseguiu salvar fotos de sua infância.

A família foi para a casa de um amigo, mas precisou sair novamente por causa da expansão do incêndio. Mais tarde, no sábado, recebeu a confirmação de que a própria casa havia sido destruída.

Casa no topo da montanha também foi destruída

Rick Arrate morava sozinho em Peavine Mountain, uma área elevada com vista para Reno e Sparks. Sua neta, Jaida Hargrove, contou que os bombeiros tentaram proteger a casa usando máquinas, cortando árvores e aplicando retardante de fogo.

“Todos achavam que ficaria tudo bem. Então, em cerca de 30 minutos, o vento mudou e o fogo chegou rápido demais”, disse Hargrove.

Arrate e os bombeiros foram obrigados a deixar a montanha.

Segundo a neta, ele só conseguiu levar consigo seus dois cães da raça golden retriever.

Arrate passou a noite de sábado na casa dos pais de Hargrove. Ainda não sabia quais seriam os próximos passos.

Campanhas de arrecadação foram criadas na internet para ajudar Arrate e a família Kieffer.

Tyler Duvall estava acampando no fim de semana e disse que o incêndio parecia pequeno na manhã de sábado.

No dia seguinte, sua casa já estava dentro da área de evacuação.

“O vento realmente fez o fogo crescer”, afirmou.

Somente no sábado, 15 novos incêndios foram registrados em diferentes pontos de Nevada.

O período de seca e a quantidade recorde de neve registrada neste inverno no oeste dos Estados Unidos contribuíram para criar condições favoráveis à propagação das chamas.

No início deste mês, incêndios no leste do estado de Washington obrigaram cerca de 60 mil pessoas a deixarem suas casas na região de Spokane

Outros três incêndios ao norte de Reno também haviam provocado a retirada de mais de 13 mil moradores.

Novo morador de Reno enfrenta sequência de desastres

Ted Melden, policial e bombeiro aposentado, mudou-se com a mulher para Reno no início deste mês. Desde então, enfrentou uma tempestade de granizo com alagamentos, dois apagões e, agora, o segundo incêndio na região em duas semanas.

Melden morava anteriormente na Carolina do Sul. Durante os dois anos em que viveu no estado, passou pelos efeitos do furacão Helene e de um tornado que causou danos em seu bairro.

Por enquanto, ele não recebeu uma ordem para deixar a própria casa. Mesmo assim, já está com as malas prontas.

“Você só precisa seguir o fluxo e estar preparado”, afirmou.

David Barb também encontrou uma cena de destruição ao voltar de uma viagem de caça no fim de semana. O incêndio destruiu sua loja de taxidermia.

A casa dele, porém, foi preservada. Segundo Barb, funcionários de uma empresa de jardinagem abriram uma faixa de contenção que ajudou a impedir que as chamas chegassem ao imóvel.

A mulher de Barb estava em casa quando o incêndio começou do outro lado da montanha. Depois, ela deixou o local e foi para a casa de um amigo.

“Estou devastado, mas, graças a Deus, todos estão seguros”, disse Barb.

Locais próximos à área de evacuação monitoram o avanço das chamas

A Universidade de Nevada estava fora da área de evacuação neste domingo. Cerca de 20 mil estudantes haviam se mudado para as residências universitárias durante o fim de semana.

Dois hospitais retiraram pacientes da região.

O xerife também afirmou que as autoridades monitoravam de perto a situação para decidir se seria necessário retirar os presos da cadeia do condado.

Fumaça sobe ao longe enquanto um incêndio florestal atinge Reno. — Foto: Haven Daley / AP
